speechtext: This bill is most difficult for the house to consider, for this reason. The minister, with obvious sincerity I think, assures us that he requires the powers contained in the bill in order properly to administer his department. Any minister coming to the house with a claim of that character necessarily commands our sympathy and attention. I believe he has given very earnest thought to this measure; but there are certain features contained in it which we must most carefully consider. My main objection is that in part, if not in its entirety, the bill departs from the principle of appointment through the Civil Service Commission, and what is known as the merit system. I am aware that my statement may be called in question as regards the merit system, because the minister declares-I think sincerely-that he is desirous of making appointments. It is pretty hard, Mr. Chairman, to talk against the whole house. If we cannot have better-attention I shall sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I say the minister might very properly challenge the last statement, claiming that he is proposing this method of appointment in the interests of efficiency. However, I wish to -bring to the attention of the committee some matters in connection with this very drastic and serious change which I believe ought to be considered most carefully before we agree to the bill.
Let me say in a general way that I would not see so much objection to the bill if the
National Revenue Act

process proposed permitted the appointments to be made by the Civil Service Commission in consultation with the minister. But unfortunately the bill does not so provide. It really places the power of appointment practically entirely in the hands of the minister, and the Civil Service Commission are reduced to the rather invidious (position of being invited to acquiesce; if they do not acquiesce, then there is no remedy so far as' they are concerned. If the principle of appointment were changed so that the appointments were made by the Civil Service Commission in consultation with himself or his officers, a large measure of the Objection would be removed.
I think it desirable to bring to the attention of the committee certain evidence, if I may so term it. For instance, I propose to quote briefly from an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press, for it is indicative of what is the opinion of the informed public. Quoting the Winnipeg Free Press, I shall at least be acquitted of any desire to be partisan. The Winnipeg Free Press, on May 2, in a rather lengthy editorial, from which I shall read only one or two excerpts, has this to say:
The country will keep a sharp eye on the move made at Ottawa to remove the appointment of certain officials of the Department of National Revenue, mainly in the Customs department, from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission.
Then they go on with quite a long argument on the subject, which I shall not read but which is very interesting and, I think, illuminating. They conclude the editorial
with these two paragraphs:
Outside of party heelers, this country is pretty well satisfied with the work and functions of the Civil Service Commission. It offers equal opportunity for all young Canadians to enter the service of their country if they have the necessary qualifications. It is a safe guess that the merit system has brought into the service a better qualified and more energetic type of young man and woman than ever came in under the patronage way of handing out government jobs. Any action at Ottawa that appears to strike a blow at the underpinning of the merit system is likely to be regarded with grave suspicion throughout the country. The present government at Ottawa is reasonably suspected of itching to get its hands on civil service patronage. Its record in this respect is not altogether aboveboard, due largely to the performances of the Postmaster General, which is one reason why the public will be highly suspicious of the present move that would give the cabinet minister the authority to hire anyone to whom he might take a fancy, or who might be forced on him by local party organizations. The government would be well advised to leave civil service appointments to the body set up by parliament to attend to that department of the national service.

Some hon. gentlemen laugh, but these are not my own observations; I am quoting from an editorial in the Free Press for what it may be worth.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not like to interrupt,
but I think that editorial was based on the resolution itself, which went a great deal further than the bill. I have heard no adverse comments, nor comments of any kind, since the introduction of the bill itself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My object in reading the editorial, and in the remarks I am about to make, is to establish the statement I have made, namely, that we must preserve the status of the Civil Service Commission. That is my point; that is the light in which we should consider the bill.
I wish now to quote briefly from the observations of certain individual members of the government. I shall quote now from Hansard, page 2847, May 2, 1921, in which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), then leader of the opposition, is reported, criticising what was known as the Spinney bill. That bill, as hon. members will recall, removed from the Civil Service Commission certain classifications. Whether that was right or wrong is not the point; what I intend to show is the opinion which the present Prime Minister held at that time. He said:
This bill specifies three classes of appointments which are to be taken out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission and transferred to the government, thereby permitting the government's followers, in all certainty, to make recommendations which the governor in council will act upon. That is a step entirely in the wrong direction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What government introduced that bill?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Let me assure the Prime Minister that I am shielding no one. The bill was introduced in 1921 by the Conservative government, when the right hon. gentleman was leader of the opposition. It was introduced by the Union government, and my right hon. friend was then speaking as leader of the opposition. Now, we have before us to-day a parallel case: the government of the day proposes, to use the Prime Minister's own words, to take certain specified classes of appointments out of the control of the Civil Service Commission. And this he described on that occasion as "a step entirely in the wrong direction". I am merely giving his own words. On the public platform in 1926, the Prime Minister also said, according to the Ottawa Citizen:

I stand strongly, and have always stood, for the merit system and promotion on a basis of merit, and will do my utmost to see that that is maintained.
That was what the Prime Minister said at that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT

Before my
hon. friend leaves me, may I ask him whether there is not this difference in the present case, that what the government is now suggesting is to carry out the findings of a royal commission appointed to improve the customs service? This is one of the suggested improvements; at any rate it is what the commission have recommended.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I shall come to the royal commission in a moment. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister's statement is scarcely correct. I am not desirous of being too narrow in my criticisms, but the right hon. gentleman's observation is not quite accurate. But at the moment I am merely showing what the Prime Minister had to say in the past as regards the principle that should govern, whether it might be the government of that day or any other government. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on the same occasion made this statement:
I do not believe in political patronage.
I commend that to the colleagues of the hon. gentleman, the present Minister of Justice.
Mr. MfcINTOSH:	What about your own
colleagues?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT

Not a bit. My hon. friend will have the floor shortly, but the interjection was not very apt, to say the least. The present Minister of Justice, as I was saying, made this statement in 1921:
I do not believe in political patronage. It has been tried in many countries in the world, and it has been found wanting everywhere.
The present Minister of National Revenue, on the same occasion, had this remark to make:
So far as I am personally concerned, I am opposed to the system of political patronage as it obtained in the past. . . . The Civil Service Act may have its drawbacks, but even then its advantages, in my opinion, far outweigh its disadvantages.
That statement was made by the minister who is proposing the bill now before us. Now I come to the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Eorke)-and I am glad he is in his seat. I
invite him to listen to his own observations. Mark you, the Minister of Immigration is in accord with this bill and is supporting the change therein proposed. On February 2, 1923-Hansard, page 41-the present Minister of Immigration said there must be no return to patronage:
A return to patronage is unthinkable.
I ask the hon. gentleman to cogitate on that statement while he sits sombrely in his seat. Then the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) this year made the following statement, referring even to labourers on canals:
I would be very happy to have the whole situation left to the Civil Service Commission.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) was chairman of a parliamentary committee which in 1923 reported as follows:
Your committee is of the opinion that the two fundamental principles of the Civil Service Act are the merit system and the system of appointment by competitive examination, and that both these principles must be preserved.
I have read these opinions for the purpose of placing before the government the position which its own members have taken from time to time in regard to this question. Now I wish to turn to a reason advanced by the minister, and which I think had a good deal of influence on members of the house, when the resolution was under consideration the other day. The Minister of National Revenue, discussing the matter on May 8, referred particularly to appraisers. He said to the house:
And remember, these were appointed by the Civil Service Commission.
He was dealing with the report of the parliamentary committee of 1926 investigating the Customs department, and he was speaking of those who were recommended for disciplinary treatment or for discharge, stating that they were appointed by the Civil Service Commission. I have before me the names of those gentlemen who were included in that report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not think I made
reference to any particular persons at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister referred to
the report of the committee and to those persons recommended for discharge. He had particular reference to appraisers when he asked the house to bear in mind that all these gentlemen had been appointed by the Civil Service Commission. At the time I was a little doubtful as to the accuracy of his statement and the soundness of his position. I am not going to read the names of these men because I do not think it desirable to
National Revenue Act

put their names on Hansard; they have been dealt with once and we should let them go, although if it is requested I will read them. I have before me the names of nine men, not one of whom was appointed by the Civil Service Commission, all having been appointed under the old patronage system. When the minister brings forth the argument that there has been dissatisfaction with certain persons, that they were appointed by the Civil Service Commission and that therefore he would change the system, then I suggest that this point be kept in mind. These men were not appointed by the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman
permit me to interrupt? I do not pretend for one moment to disclaim any responsibility for anything I may have said the other day, but I say to him now that when I made that statement I did not have in mind any particular persons, and certainly not the persons to whom he refers. I had in mind that the appraisal system was not what it should be, and that the appraisers in general had been appointed by the Civil Service Commission. I was not referring to these particular men at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, and I say this because I am trying to be fair with the minister, when he makes a statement such as he undoubtedly made at page 2782 of Hansard to the effect that these men were appointed by the Civil Service Commission, he should be sure of his facts. That is all I desire to establish in that regard.
Now I want to come for a moment to the question of the appointment of appraisers, and whether or not it is desirable that they should be appointed altogether apart from the Civil Service Commission. In the same discussion which took place on May 8, the minister made this statement:
My opinion is that the Dominion appraisers . . . . are best qualified to make selections.
What method would be followed and what process would be adopted by the Civil Service Commission in making these appointments? I am informed that the method is this: A civil service board of examiners would be appointed, and in this instance one member of that board undoubtedly would be a Dominion appraiser. That is, they take an officer of the department affected by the appointment; if it were the preventive service the chief preventive officer would be a member of the board, and for the appraisal service undoubtedly it would be a member of the Dominion appraisers. Included in that board

would be a representative of the private business affected by the appointment; in other words, if a drygoods appraiser were to be selected, undoubtedly a member of the board would be a representative business man in the drygoods trade; then there would be a member of the civil service examining board and a representative of the Canadian Legion, who would have no vote but merely a voice in the committee to protect the interests of the returned men. That is the process adopted, and I submit to the minister that with a board of that kind selecting the appraisers, bearing in mind the fact that a representative of the board of Dominion appraisers would be a member of that board, then the Civil Service commission may well be entrusted with this task. I would be willing to say this: If after such a board decided on a certain person as being suitable for the position, while the minister was firmly convinced and had good reason to believe that such an appointee would not be suitable for the position, then I am prepared to say that the minister might have some remedy by which he could extricate himself from that difficulty. But if these appointments are to be made by the reverse process, if the minister is authorized to say to the Civil Service Commission, "Here is a man whom I want as a drygoods appraiser," and then if the Civil Service Commission refuse to appoint that man after examination, the minister can insist on the appointment, I submit that is merely a method of eliminating the Civil Service Commission and its authority.
Now we come to what the Prime Minister mentioned a moment ago, and in this connection I have before me a report which was tabled' on May 7 last. This is the report of a sub-committee appointed by the then Minister of Customs, when I held the office, for the purpose of examining into the system and organization of the Customs department in Ottawa. This committee was known as an advisory or consultative committee consisting of Mr. Dilworth, of Clarkson, Gordon and Dilworth; the chairman of the Civil Service Commission, the Auditor General of Canada, Mr. Breadner, who is now the commissioner of customs and Mr. Taylor, commissioner of excise. This was the committee appointed by the government at that time to examine into the Customs department and to recommend a method of reorganization, and I want to say that the report they made will well repay study. This report, in so far as it deals with the subject now under discussion, differs from the report of the royal commission which, as the minister correctly stated, frankly said that these selections should be made indepen-

dent of the 'Civil Service Commission. I submit to the house, without going into an examination of the report of the royal commission for the moment, that the final report did no great credit to that commission; I submit that it has every evidence of having been hastily prepared. There was an interim report dealing with specific cases which is very much more worthy of attention and study than the final report. The report of this advisory and consultative committee has this to say:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Was that the report made by Clarkson, Gordon and Dilworth?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, this is a report which was tabled on May 7 and which has not been printed. I think hon. members would do well to secure it and read it carefully, because it is perhaps the best of the series of reports which have been made on this subject. Under the heading "Selection and Appointment of Preventive Staff" a paragraph is included which is very interesting, on one or two points of which I will lay some particular stress:
As the men on this work have to work often on their own judgment and initiative and to act at times with the greatest promptness and without first reporting to their superior officers, their selection should be most carefully made and have regard to their intelligence, integrity, capacity and general suitability to the work and to no other consideration. For this reason we most strongly recommend that the selection be made by the Civil Service Commission and the chief of the preventive service.
Then they refer to the report of the special committee which made recommendations in a similar vein.
-and that the chief of the preventive service should have full power to remove for cause any officer or other employee while temporarily employed.
That is the recommendation of the special committee, composed of the gentlemen to whom I have referred, and who gave this subject careful study. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that is the course that should be followed. Let the preventive officers and the appraisers be selected by the Civil Service Commission, the former in consultation with the chief of the preventive staff and the latter in consultation with the Dominion appraisal board. Let the investigators also be selected by the Civil Service Commission, in consultation with the head of the advisory staff. In all these cases the minister is certainly to be consulted; that is, he is ex officio in all these conferences.
Now, I wish to deal with another feature of this matter. The other day the minister declared that there was no desire to interfere with the principle of appointments by the Civil Service Commission. I am not desirous of attacking the minister's good faith, because I appreciate that he is labouring under most difficult circumstances. We credit him with an earnest desire to make the best appointments possible, but the house must remember that when enacting a statute of this kind we are laying down a system that will be followed by other ministers than the present incumbent of office. At the present moment, under the stress of the last couple of years of scrutiny and investigation of the department, it is quite likely that the minister will bestir himself to keep within the bounds of-what shall I say, decency?-but when things have quieted down and we get a little farther away from the cause of revision of this section of the civil service system, it follows, I think, as a matter of course that we simply go back to the patronage system, in all its simplicity and with all its evils. Undoubtedly the patronage system had more evil attached to it than merit. Appointments under the patronage system are made for the purpose-I think I can put it simply and plainly-of giving jobs to those who are in favour with the ministry of the day, whatever ministry it is. It may be argued that under that system good appointments have been and will be made. I am not disputing that, but the point is that the principle-or lack of principle-is in that it is for service to a given party, whatever party happens to be in power at the time.
Years ago we departed from or abandoned the patronage system. My own opinion is that we went too hurriedly, and in our efforts to install or inauguarate a complete system of civil service in Canada we laid on the Civil Service Commission at the commencement too heavy a task, and it has taken years to build up an equitable and reasonable system. I do not suggest for a moment that the civil service system as we now have it is entirely satisfactory. They are human, and undoubtedly they have made mistakes. In connection with the appointments to which I referred as not being made by the Civil Service Commission, the minister might very well say to me, "Hold on, some of those were undoubtedly promoted by the Civil Service Commission of the day." That was disclosed in the inquiry, and it was brought out in a manner that led to the retirement of two of the commissioners. Undoubtedly the Civil Service Commission is not without the possibility of fault. We do not assert that. These two commisisoners were retired, and replaced by two others; and I think it was because
National Revenue Act

they had more or less trafficked in the question of promotions. It showed the resentment of parliament and of the country against such a procedure by a civil service commissioner; it does not challenge the soundness of the system that two gentlemen went somewhat wrong in the discharge of their duty.
And so I say to the minister that so far as I am concerned I am opposed to this bill to the extent that it departs from the principle of appointment by the Civil Service Commission. I say again to him, as I said in my opening remarks, that if this bill were so drafted that the appointments should be made by the Civil Service Commission in consultation with the head of the branch to which the appointee is to be sent, then I have little objection to it. But in its present form, where the Civil Service Commission play no major or primary part in appointments, I am opposed to it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just a word to say in answer to my hon. friend. I have listened to his remarks with great attention. I know the first officer of the Department of National Revenue very well. I am not acquainted with the commissioner of customs, but I know he is a most remarkable man. When Mr. Good called a meeting of the public accounts committee some years ago, Mr. Breadner was asked some questions. He had apparently no information with him, but he answered them from memory, and I think he answered them very successfully. He is a very straightforward man, and I am pleased to say the same thing about Mr. Taylor, the commissioner of excise, and also of Mr. Walters, the commissioner of income tax. These three gentlemen are very able men; I do not think anyone will question their ability. But they were appointed not by the Civil Service Commission, but by the Minister of National Revenue, and he deserves praise for that. I remember at the time that I read several editorials in Tory as well as Liberal papers, congratulating him on those appointments. I do not believe any member will come back at me when I say that one of those papers was the Ottawa Journal, which is not a Liberal paper. I remember also that the Montreal Gazette published editorials, praising the minister. We must not overlook the fact, that the task of the Minister of National Revenue is a rather ungrateful one. because instead of spending money he has to collect it. He has met with very good success, and the amount of the last surplus collections, $14,000,000, should be considered. The Department of National Revenue is directed by an able minister, assisted by able

men, and those men can be entrusted with the confidence of parliament. No one can reproach them for doing anything they should not do. They are upright men; they do their duty well; they are conscientious, and I am sure they are acting to t'he best of their ability. I am not in the habit of paying compliments to people but I take this opportunity of saying all the good I think of them. In such matters as these every member is entitled to say a word about the competency of the man who applies for any of the positions to which this legislation refers. Anyone who is recommended should merit that recommendation and no one knows better the character and competency of the applicant than the member for the constituency in which such an officer is to be appointed. When a man is recommended by a member as being an able person, the minister knows that recommendation is worthy of consideration and he acts accordingly. I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) who now is afraid of the bill, who thinks it will not work well, will at t'he next session praise the minister for having brought such a measure before the house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Subsection 4 reads:
The minister may, after such examination as he may prescribe-
The minister is going to prescribe the examination. There is to be no provision in the bill as to how the examination will take place. The bill does not state that the minister shall take any particular line of action to secure a board of examiners and he may do the examining himself.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre has already placed on the record the opinions expressed by different members of the cabinet in years gone by and it is very illuminating to notice the change of front which they take now that they are in office as opposed to the

Referring back to the customs inquiry committee I believe it is reasonably understood -and I have heard no criticism to the contrary-that practically all the men who were retired as not giving the proper service that they were expected to give to the country, were to all intents and purposes appointed under the patronage system. Possibly some of them were promoted from the ranks, but primarily they were appointed under the patronage system and not by the Civil Service Commission. There is no doubt the Civil Service Commission is the proper body to make these selections, and when the resolution was under consideration before the house a few days ago I suggested it would be advisable for the minister to allow the commission, with proper representation from the board of supervisors on the examining board, to make the appointments. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I cannot let the opportunity go by without saying that I oppose the bill because, notwithstanding the assurance given by the minister, it is nothing more than an attempt to return to the patronage system in regard to the appointment of these particular officers. If this principle is adopted in regard to these officials of the department it may equally be applied to other officials and employees in the same department. More than that, this same principle can be extended on exactly the same reasoning to other departments of the government. The principle involved is whether appointments shall be made by the minister. The minister, of course no matter how fine a man he may be, no matter how intelligent and capable he may be, no matter what qualifications he has for making appointments, is necessarily lacking in information in regard to the fitness of the applicants for the positions, and he must act upon the recommendations which he will receive. This particular service extends all over Canada. It may be that so far as Ottawa is concerned the head officials of the department may be able to advise the minister as to the proper officers to be appointed, but what about the rest of Canada?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Certainly not; I do
not believe in it; I do not think it is right in principle, and that is why I am opposing this bill. I know the desire that there is on the other side of the house for the abolition of the Civil Service Commission altogether. There are a great many members over there who desire to get back to patronage; there is no doubt about that at all, and they say that they are in a better position to make recommendations for appointments than any
[Mr. Euler. 1
civil service commission can be. That is the principle that is involved here, and if you do this now, you are simply inserting the thin edge of the wedge, and on exactly the same reasoning you can apply this same principle to all other departments of the government, and so get away entirely from the Civil Service Commission.
I know that there is great objection to this bill taken by the civil service organizations.
I have received communications from the organization in my constituency, and they at least look upon this as an attempt to return to the patronage system.
Let us consider for a moment just what the situation is at the present time in regard to appointments. Appointments are made by the Civil Service Commission upon the results of examinations which are held in accordance with the regulations, examinations which have been worked out after a number of years of experience. That does not mean that the department has nothing to say in regard to the appointments. In the first place, if appointments are made which are not acceptable to the department or to the minister, he can refuse to accept the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission. In the next place when the examinations are conducted, the officers of the department usually have something to say in setting those examinations, and in fact, they conduct them to a certain extent. In all the large centres all over Canada the officers of this department and of other departments have a good deal to do with the holding of examinations. More than that, in regard to promotions, which come under the head of appointments, the Civil Service Commission is guided to a large extent by the ratings which are recommended by the officers of the department involved, and appointments are usually made according to those ratings. It does not seem to me that that is objectionable in any way.
T do think that this bill is wrong in principle entirely. It is objectionable not only to the civil servants of this country, but to the public generally. It is a step in the wrong direction. It is nothing more or less than inserting the thin end of the wedge, and the minister is attempting to do that under the guise of the necessities of this particular department, which are no greater than the necessities of a great many other departments of this government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I wish to say just a few
words, not many at this late stage of the . session, on this bill. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat says that this is the thin edge of the wedge. I am a little afraid that

it is the thick edge of the wedge, because for some time now we have been getting a good deal of this in the various departments. The other day I asked some questions on the order paper regarding the appointment of a postmaster in a little village in the western part of Ontario, somewhere near Sarnia; I do not remember the county or the town at the moment, but I do happen to know the facts, and the facts were that a returned soldier was recommended for the position by the Civil Service Commission, and yet in spite of that, the Postmaster General overruled the commission's recommendation and appointed somebody else that suited him. Referring to this matter, I said to the Postmaster General, as reported in Hansard, of May 3:
The reason I asked the question is that I have just received a reply to a question on to-day's order paper showing that the Civil Service Commission recommended a returned soldier for a job, and my hon. friend and his department refused to accept him.
And the Postmaster General replied:
Under the act the Postmaster General has the power to refuse to accept the certificate of the commission, but the act does not give him power to classify the employees.
In other words, at the present time on some occasions at least, if not on many, recommendations of the Civil Service Commission are being ignored by some of the departments. The minister who is conducting this bill came into the house at the same time I did, eleven years ago, and during the many years when he was just an ordinary member of the house and a supporter of the government, he was quite independent in his attitude because I remember him on one or two occasions voting against his party. That takes courage; I tried it myself once or twice, and I know something about it. At any rate, the minister, of whom personally I am very fond, is not showing in this bill, I think, the same independence that used to characterize him in the days before the lus't of office reached him. He is, I think, building up for himself troubles which he may have difficulty in overcoming, because as these positions are thrown open he will find members on his side of the house seeking positions for friends of theirs, and if-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

In all seriousness I regret to see him laying up this store of trouble for himself, for undoubtedly that is what he is doing.
Referring again to the patronage system, during all the years I have been in the house, whether one party or the other was in power, this system to a large extent did not exist.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I say that seriously. The patronage system of appointments has largely not obtained within the last ten or eleven years. The system may now exist; that probably is what my hon. friends are laughing at. I mean that up till recently the patronage system had not been resorted to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If there was no patronage system in operation, how does my hon. friend account for the fact that all the postmasters appointed in my constituency after 1911 were Tories?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Undoubtedly the government of the day picked out the very best men that they could find in the constituency. But I must confess that seeing my hon. friend on that side of the chartfber I wonder how, with so many good Conservatives in that section, he was returned to the house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I wonder at it myself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: They are mostly all in the post offices.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: To members who have entered the house in recent years, I desire to say that patronage is to a large extent simply work cast upon the shoulders of the member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Take my own experience. I do not presume, although mine is a very fine constituency, that the people there are higher minded than elsewhere, but they do not bother me for positions. To-day practically all appointments are made by the Civil Service Commission, and this has been the practice since the formation of the commission. I find that with rare exceptions the people are satisfied with this method. I believe a similar condition exists throughout the country to a large extent, and that the
National Revenue Act

people by and large heartily approve of the elimination of the old patronage system, although probably it was abused more than it deserved to be. In this view our people are in harmony with public opinion in England, the United States and other countries. Because of this strong public opinion in favour of the merit system under the Civil Service Commission, I think the iminster should hesitate long before going back to a system which, rightly or wrongly, has become discredited. On the whole I believe the Civil Service Commission have given the country reasonably satisfactory service, and whatever faults they may have-and no doubt no commission is perfect-those faults are few and slight compared with the condition of affairs under the old system. I repeat, by this bill the minister is laying up a store of troubles, and I think later on he will deeply regret not leaving these appointments almost entirely in the hands of the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Suppose two men equally qualified applied to my hon. friend for a position, one a partisan, the other a non-partisan, which man would he appoint?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I say without any hesitation at all that if I were making the appointment, and the partisan was just as good a man for the position as the non-partisan applicant, I would without question appoint my friend. Please note, I say if I had the making of the appointment. The appointment should foe left to the Civil Service Commission. But let me remind my hon. friend who is such a loyal supporter of the Prime Minister, that on one occasion I heard the right hon. gentleman abuse us on this side as though we were pickpockets because we had the temerity to appoint Conservatives to the Senate. In his view that was one of our greatest crimes. At a meeting a few days later I frankly stated that I wondered if he expected us to appoint Liberals. That was the idealistic attitude taken by my right hon. friend, and in view of his opinions in those days I think he should support me in my stand that the Minister of National Revenue should leave to the Civil Service Commission the appointments dealt with in this bill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There is always sound
