maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I raise my
voice in protest against this bill. Subsection four of section one provides that:
The minister may, after such examination as he may prescribe, select and nominate suitable persons for appointment by the Civil Service Commission.
In my opinion nothing could be better calculated to undermine the work of the Civil Service Commission. Year after year we have seen numbers of civil servants withdrawn from the control of the Civil Service Commission. These withdrawals total several thousand, and sim'ply mean a return to the old patronage plan. I realize that in this we are face to face with one of the most important but intricate functions of government-the control of the civil service. Having at great expense set up the machinery for the filling of all offices in the civil service, we find whichever party happens to foe in power year after year taking away from the control of the Civil Service Commission many civil servants.
I am surprised at the Minister of National Revenue bringing in a measure of this kind, for only lately I read his sentiments regarding this question as expressed by him in 1921. I believe with the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) that what the minister is seeking will undoubtedly lead him into trouble. The whole country is alarmed at the attitude which the government is taking towards the Civil Service Commission, and I shall be only doing my duty by reading a letter which I have received from the Saskatchewan Customs and Excise Officials' Association. This is dated April 27, and is as follows:
As you are no doubt aware the honourable the Minister of National Revenue introduced a resolution in the house on the 30th ultimo seeking to amend the Department of National Revenue Act granting authority to enable him:
(a)	To appoint and pay certain officers (appraisers, special excise officers, investigators of values and drawbacks, etc.).
(b)	To grant gratuities to officers in lieu of leave of absence, in order to permit replacing such officers so retired immediately.
(e) To arrange such promotions and transfers as are in the public interest.
The adoption of this would be a radical departure from the present system of making appointments through the Civil Service Commission, so far as paragraphs (a) and (c) are concerned; with paragraph (b) we are in accord.
This association views the resolution with deep apprehension, and cannot conceive of it as being in the best interests of civil service reform. We further believe it to be unnecessary, as the method of filling vacancies, promotions, etc., administered under the Civil Service Act at present is adequate and just to all concerned.

National Revenue Act
1 have been asked by this association to lay our views before you on this matter, trusting I am not assuming too great a liberty, and that your view on this may agree with ours.
I am,
Yours very truly,
T. W. McPhail,
President, Sask. C. & E. 0. Assoc.
The government, in my opinion, is taking a retrograde step. For many years, in the west particularly, farmers' associations have had as one of their chief planks the abolition of patronage. I view with apprehension the present proposal and, I repeat, the government is taking a retrograde step. With others who have spoken against the proposal I therefore protest against the bill in its present form.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Why is the minister using the name of the Civil Service Commission in the bill as draughted, leaving them without power? Why did he not bring in a bill simply to give the government power and the minister authority to appoint these men, not mentioning the Civil Service Commission at all?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
When the resolution was
under discussion the other day, I think I explained the provisions of the bill fairly fully, and I believe I also anticipated to a large extent the objections that have been raised to-day. For that reason I do not propose to review them at any length; but I might perhaps make one or two observations, called forth by some of the remarks we have just heard. Let me deal in the first place with the question raised by my hon. friend (Sir George Perley) which was asked the other day and to which I replied. The hon. gentleman asks why, instead of taking the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, the minister does not himself make the appointment. That is the question as I understand it. I said the other day, and I say again, that this provision was included at the suggestion of some of my friends in this house who felt that if the minister were obliged to make a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission it would at least act as a check, or a brake, as I described it then, upon him if he desired to make any political appointments. That is the sole purpose of the insertion of this requirement, that the nomination shall go first to the Civil Service Commission. Moreover, it places on them a certain responsibility, and, after that, a responsibility on the minister and the government itself, because the minister himself
does not make the appointment. Even if the Civil Service Commission declines to make the appointment it goes to the governor in council, and that again constitutes a second brake upon the activities of the minister if he is exercising them in a wrongful way.
I really propose to answer only one objection-the main objection. I believe there is only one objection, and that is that this is an attempt to interfere with or to wipe out the principle of the Civil Service Commission. Let me say that this is not such an attempt; it is not intended to interfere with the principle under which the Civil Service Commission operates. And this is not the first occasion on which an exception has been made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does not the minister
think that while it may not be his intention- I do not believe it is his intenuon- -to open the uoor to patronage, it aciually does open the door to any future minister who may wish to take advantage of it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will
permit me to go on I will answer that question. That is not a departure at all. There are exceptions to practically all rules. The mere fact that there is an exception presupposes that there is a rule, and the rule is not abolished because an exception is made to it. Some years ago, after the Civil Service Commission had been established and after the Civil Service Act of 1918 had been passed, I was a member of the house when, in 1921, an effort was made by the then government, the Union government, in what was known as the Spinney bill, to make exceptions which were far wider in their scope than this little bill of mine. In fact, as I remember-and I was a member of the committee that considered that bill-the Spinney bill proposed that the appointment of certain technical officers throughout the whole service, not only in the Customs department, but in the entire service, should be removed from the control of the Civil Service Commission and be vested again in the ministers, under what you may term patronage, if you care to do so.
The statement has been made to-day that the minister has reversed his position-that although I have been always in favour of the Civil Service Commission I have changed my mind. Now, if my experience showed me that I was wrong in anything, I hope I should have the courage to admit that I was wrong and that I should not be afraid to say that I had changed my mind. But in this particular I have not changed my mind. I can quote from the very speech from which the hon.
National Revenue Act

member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and, I believe, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) quoted, to show what attitude I then took. I quote the following:
I understand-
I said.
-that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) proposes another amendment to the effect that during the recess the deputy ministers and the Civil Service Commission may get together to decide as to what other employees should properly be exempted from the operations of the commission.
Quite plainly there was an effort then to remove from the control of the Civil Service Commission certain employees. I said:
Now, I quite agree with that suggestion- I made it myself-
I had made it in committee.
-but there is this difference between us: the minister would give the commission power to make these exemptions, in other words, to have an accomplished fact and to report to parliament. My contention was that they in their wisdom should come to a decision so far as was thought advisable in regard to what changes should be made, but that they should not have the final say, but should come with their recommendations to parliament, and that then parliament should deal with those recommendations on their merits.
That is exactly the position I take to-day. The exemptions we make to-day do not go so far as the exemptions then proposed, and my proposal is that parliament, rather than the Civil Service Commission, shall pass upon them. I am to-day just as much in favour of the principle of the Civil Service Commission as I have been at any time, but I hope I do not propose to drive a theory to an absurd conclusion if experience shows me that there may be advantage in a slight modification of it. And the fact that there is some modification of it does not, I contend, destroy the principle.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it not a fact that this bill will eliminate the preference which is given, under the Civil Service Act, to returned men? Would the minister consider a suggestion that he provide in this bill that this preference shall be retained?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have answered that question before. There is no intention on the part either of the minister or of the department to discriminate against returned men. Other things being equal, they are supposed to get the same preference now as they got before. And the sp,me applies to those already in the service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Will the minister put that in his bill?
[Mr. Euler.I

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, I will not. As I have already said, there is only one reason for this bill. Until some months ago the customs department was being severely criticized for inefficiency and other things; it was criticized by parliament, by a parliamentary committee, by the press and more recently by a royal commission which investigated that department. Many changes have been made, I think for the benefit of the service; in accordance with some of the recommendations made by the commission the department sees other ways in which improvements can be made in the service, and I hope hon. members of the committee will believe that is our only purpose in introducing this bill and suggesting these changes, which are very moderate in themselves. With that I think every member of the committee will agree, although I will admit that there may be honest differences of opinion as to the method which should be followed.
As I have already said, the bill is very moderate in its scope; it does not go nearly so far as the recommendations of the royal commission. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre quoted from the report of a committee appointed by himself, which I continued after I came into office; the report of that committee does not agree entirely with the reports of other committees. We have another body known as the Commercial Protective Association, which took an entirely different view, going even further than anything we have embodied in this bill. Better than that, and I think I may say that fairly, a deliberative body was appointed by this government consisting of three judges, who made a most exhaustive investigation extending over about a year; they recommended that the minister be given control over these appointments as well as over appointments to branches of the department other than appraisers and investigators. Although this may be contradicted in a sense, the minister takes no responsibility and no power for making these appointments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Will the minister repeat
that last statement?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister takes no power to make appointments himself; he first makes recommendations to the commission. As far as I am concerned, and I think this would be carried out by any other minister, that course will be followed, and I think the house should admit that when men come into positions of responsibility they at least feel that responsibility to the country and are not constantly thinking of ways to exercise politi-

National Revenue Act

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There is also the preventive service.
cal patronage and so on. If in order to obtain the results we all desire in connection with the reorganization of the department it is necessary to depart in a small degree from the exercise of a general principle such as is contained in the Civil Service Act, I have no apology to make, and I say that quite frankly. To me, the object to be attained is more important than slavish observance of a principle not a moral principle-if it is shown that by such a slight deviation from that principle, in peculiar circumstances, we can obtain better results. Surely we should learn something from experience. I can say that in the short time I have had some responsibility in the matter I think I could make even some further suggestions than those contained in this bill, all of which would be for the benefit of the service. The point I desire to make is this: There is no attempt to drive a horse and wagon through the principle of the Civil Service Act; this bill merely establishes an exception to the general rule, as has been found advisable through experience. I might appropriately quote that old saying: "The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath." I think that applies equally in this case; I am not criticizing the Civil Service Commission, but it was made for the good of the public service, and the public service was not made for the good of the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would just ask a question there. Let us suppose that next year one of the minister's colleagues wishes to bring in a similar bill with regard to his own department in order to control appointments. What would the minister say?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If he could make a case
as good as I think I am making I believe parliament should grant his request. Now let us see for a few moments what is actually in the bill to which so much objection has been taken. It proposes that out of the 5,500 odd employees of this department some 200 or possibly 250 positions shall be taken from under the control of the Civil Service Commission. There are not more than 250 appraisers and special investigators throughout the service, not only in Ottawa but in the various ports throughout the Dominion. Most of these men will remain where they are; I do not even say that any of them will 'be removed from the place they now occupy, so only a small percentage of those people now occupyipg the position of appraisers will be actually affected by the enactment of this law.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, but that is now under
the control of the minister, and the minister proposes to take that away from himself and give it to the governor in council.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I will come to that in a moment. He is doing that because he desires to exercise patronage as little as possible, although I am afraid my friends will not believe that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Afraid to be responsible for these appointments?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As I have said, for these positions, which-outside the preventive service, which is already under the control of the minister-total some 200 or 250 officers, the minister may make a selection, nominate a man, and recommend him to the Civil Service Commission, which shall make the appointment within a stated period. If the commission refuse to make the appointment, the minister makes it himself, not as recommended by the various commissions but through the governor in council. I will freely admit that the bill in effect places the power of selection and appointment of this small class of officers in the hands of the department or of the minister, if you like it that way, because if the minister has the confidence of his colleagues I should think and expect that when he makes a recommendation to his colleagues in council, in the great majority of cases they would accept that recommendation. If council did not do so I think it would be an intimation to the minister that he did not enjoy the confidence of his colleagues.
That is the one vital thing in the bill; that small class of officers in the service, the appraisers and the investigators, in effect shall be appointed by the minister, upon advice of the board of appraisers, if you like to put it that way, through the governor in council. Now the question arises as to why we should make a change in the method of appointing these appraisers. This is done primarily because of the absolutely vital importance of an efficient appraisal staff. If that staff is not what it should be, if the men are not experts skilled in the work which they have to do, the result will foe a great loss to the revenues. The tariff is based directly on valuations of goods; if these valuations are too low it is not necessary to point out that the revenues must suffer very seriously. Unless the appraisal system is excellent, and better than it is to-day, we are not going to

National Revenue Act

receive the revenues we should receive, and my protectionist friends would be justified in saying that the manufacturers of this country did not receive the protection to which they were entitled. Let us see for a moment what the different commissions and1 others think of the necessity for a proper appraisal system, although I do not desire to delay the committee at any great length because I think most hon. members are already seized of the importance of this matter. First let us consider the Contoiercial Protective Association, whose representations received very great attention from the parliamentary committee. Speaking of the board of appraisers, they say:
That the board be given power to retain such appraisers as they deem competent and qualified and to appoint, with the minister's approval, and notwithstanding the provisions of the Civil Service Act, such further appraisers as may be required from time to time-
Then a little later:
In dealing with important merchandise and in ensuring that the full duties provided for in the law are collected, it is above all things essential that there should be an efficient system of appraisal by competent appraisers.
The appraisal system is the very heart of the whole system of the collection of customs revenue, and if the appraisal system is not sound there is bound to be inefficiency and failure to detect frauds.
The Canadian appraisal system is lamentably weak. At many ports there are not a sufficient number of capable and efficient appraisers to give that prompt service which is so essential to the conduct of business. At the smaller ports men are acting as appraisers in addition to performing other duties-men who have not had the training to fit them for their duties as appraisers, and at all ports the rate of pay is so inadequate that trained experts cannot be prevailed upon to enter the service.
The parliamentary committee reported as follows:
First, the methods of appraisal are exceedingly careless and fail to safeguard the interests of the importer, or the revenues of the country from being defrauded by undervaluation, and, secondly, persons appointed as appraisers are in many instances untrained in the branch to which they are appointed.
And the royal commission reported as follows:
This question touches not only the administration at the department in Ottawa, but extends through all the ports in the Dominion.
It has been recognized and must be admitted that a proper system of appraisal lies at the very base of the customs administration. It is almost axiomatic that the staff of appraisers should possess the necessary expert and technical knowledge to enable them to discharge their duties efficiently. The present system fails to provide a staff of appraisers to meet these requirements.
Our inquiry has shown that the present system of appointing appraisers or other officers requiring expert or technical knowledge is

unsatisfactory, and we are convinced that where expert and technical knowledge is required, the examination of the applicants for positions should be conducted by those who are specially qualified to act in the premises.
We are of opinion that all appointments to the office of appraiser at the different ports of the Dominion should be made by the minister after examination of the applicants by the board of appraisers.
We quite recognize that this method of appointment would conflict with the system now in vogue under the Civil Service Act, but notwithstanding this we are of the opinion that this method should be adopted.
This was also the opinion of the Commercial Protective Association.
The present system has been wrong. It has been possible to do this, and it has been done: A man, we will say, was appointed to the position of customs truckman, an important and respectable position. Then he might be promoted to be a computing clerk, in which position he would learn about the various rates in the tariff, but he would not learn one thing about the values of goods, or the worth of commodities. And yet, that man might be, and has been, appointed to the office of appraiser in an important port. You cannot expect this man to detect undervaluation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But he could not be appointed without the approval of the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think you will find that only in a very few instances do the ministers desire to reject appointments that are made by the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There was a very good illustration of that the other day right in this city.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
You have not found very many in the Department of National Revenue. To appraise properly, a man requires to have expert knowledge of commodities, which only a skilled and qualified man possesses. I am not here to criticize the Civil Service Commission. I think they are doing a good work, but I do say this: they are not as well qualified to pass upon the merits and qualifications of appraisers as the officers of our own department. The matter of personality enters into it also to some extent. Our board of appraisers are personally acquainted with men expert in the valuation of commodities throughout the whole country. They become personally acquainted with the men that are already on the staff. I may say, to quiet the fears, perhaps, of some of our own officials, that we have no intention of calling in men from the outside if we have men in our own

National Revenue Act
service who ought to be promoted and who have full knowledge of the work we want them to do. But I will also say that if we find we have a peculiar position, a position that requires a peculiarly intimate knowledge of some particular commodity, and we cannot find the man in the service, or cannot find him among the returned men, we will have no hesitation, and I think we would be justified, in going outside to find a man that can do the work properly, and thus protect the revenues of the country.
Mr. Chairman, that is practically the whole story. The royal commission says, the Commercial Protective Association says, the executive officers of the department say, and the minister believes that competent appraisers can be selected most successfully by the experienced officers of the department. They know those within and outside of the department who are best qualified.
I just want to repeat, in conclusion, that after all the minister has delegated some of the powers that he now has, or that might have been assigned to him by the recommendations of the royal commission. This power has been delegated, in part, to the Civil Service Commission, and finally to the governor in council. The commission recommended that the auditors under the Special War Revenue Act, commonly known as the Sales Tax Act, should be appointed by the minister. The minister has not chosen to follow that recommendation, but preferred to leave it with the Civil Service Commission. I believe that the matter of the appointment of auditors will be worked out properly by the commisison. I do not desire to interfere with the function of that commission any more than seems advisable.
With regard to the preventive service. As it stands now, the special preventive service, consisting of a force of some 300 men, is appointed by the minister himself. In the future, if this bill passes, the appointments to the preventive service will be made in the same way as it is proposed to appoint appraisers and special investigators. Again, to that extent, the minister has divested himself of the powers which he has had.
I have stated before that the provisions of the bill are very moderate indeed, and we are going to observe the principle of merit and promotion. I believe in the principle of the Civil Service Commission; I cannot say that too often. I have no desire to interfere with the commission, but I also believe that there are exceptions to every rule. I do not believe in following a theory at all points
merely in order to be consistent; I believe in the exercise of common sense, where practical experience shows that the theory does not always serve the purposes of efficiency.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Why does the minister so
emphatically refuse to insert a provision similar to that in the Civil Service Act, relating to returned soldiers?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think that any bill should be burdened with too many provisions. If the minister desired not to obey that, there would be absolutely nothing to prevent him from exercising favouritism as against returned soldiers. I do not see where it would have any practical effect.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As it now stands, it gives
the minister every opportunity of exercising discrimination against returned soldiers.
_ Mr. EULER:	Which he would also have
in the other case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If there was an expressed
statutory requirement that returned soldiers should be given preference, all things being equal, the minister would be bound to give preference to returned soldiers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Who would be the judge
as to whether all other things were equal?
Mr. CLARK. That is just the point. The minister is admitting now that he is not a fit and proper judge.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am admitting nothing of
the sort.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I cannot take it to be otherwise.
Mr: EULER:	If the minister desired to
use his position in a wrongful way, to discriminate against the returned men, he could do it just as well when the provision was inserted in the bill. It would still be entirely within the judgment of the minister himself as to whether the returned men were fit for the positions. If he did not want to appoint them, he would say that he would not recommend them as fit for the positions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We may assume, at any
rate, that every minister will exercise an honest judgment, and not one of prejudice. If he does that, and if the statute requires him to give that preference, then his own honesty will dictate that course and he will give the returned soldiers the preference.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
His own honesty ought to
dictate that course anyway.
National Revenue Act

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Certainly it ought to dictate the course in any case, but if there is in the legislation a provision similar to that in the Civil Service Act, it will be a guide which will restrict all ministers to a principle; and I hope we may assume that this minister and all succeeding ministers will be honest in the way in which they carry out the spirit and intention of the act. I believe that in all the findings of the royal commission no returned soldier was involved in the customs scandal, and I think the same preference should be given to them in this regard as in employment generally throughout the civil service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am glad to say at the
outset that this is one occasion upon which I find myself in entire accord with the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans). Perhaps we have not agreed very often in the past. What has not been made clear by the minister is whether or not with his selections as proposed in the bill he is going to improve conditions. I do not see why the Civil Service Commission, properly equipped and furnishing itself with proper information necessary to fill each one of these positions, cannot make just as good a selection and perhaps a more independent one than is suggested under the bill. The admission of the minister in response to the inquiry of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) is a clean-cut indication that this is only the thin edge of the wedge, as has been suggested by some of the previous speakers. The minister replied to the effect that if some other minister next year applied to have a similar change introduced into his department and put up a good enough talk, such as our friend has done, there is no reason why that minister should not be granted the same privilege. This might be carried all the way down the line. One of the strongest recommendations for the use of the Civil Service Commission is the fact that the great body of civil servants of Canada appear to be thoroughly satisfied with the scheme and also satisfied that it is an improvement on the old patronage system.
This bill has created a good deal of speculation, and doubt, as to just how far it is proposed to proceed. It is looked on in some regards with a good deal of suspicion. I rose just in order to make very clear my position as being opposed to the return of the old patronage system. Having occupied the position of a civil servant for many years, I feel that appointments should be made as have been done in recent years, namely, by the Civil Service Commission. Civil servants should be permitted to retain their independence, and I do not know of anything more
{Mr. EulerJ
humiliating to the service than to have to approach some politician hat in hand to ask for a job for which he has every right to apply. I believe in those positions being filled by the Civil Service Commission in a clean-cut, impartial manner. So long as the Civil Service Commission makes the selection, let them select the best man and get efficiency at any cost, and let us not return to the old system of patronage which has been so unsatisfactory in the past.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I must congratulate the minister on his mode of presentation. He can say in a very mild and moderate manner the most dangerous things. That is just the trouble at the present time. He says that this is not a new departure. As a matter of fact that is quite true. Last year or the year before the minister came to parliament in the same way asking that preventive officers should be taken out of the civil service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: They were out already.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I can remember
very distinctly-and I think I am correct in saying this-that a new force was to be put on comprised of men who would not come under the civil service, and who would be freer to act than civil service appointees would be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Just to put the matter right, I think my hon. friend should understand that it was merely proposed to add to the number of the special preventive force, the nucleus of which had been appointed the year before by the minister himself. It was merely adding to that; it was not a new creation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It was a distinct
extension of the scheme and would result in putting a larger number of people outside of the civil service. I can remember some of us opposing it at the time and pointing to the disastrous results in the United States where the preventive service had been taken from under the civil service organizations and had become essentially a patronage organization. I say again, unfortunately this is not a departure, because again and again and again during the last few years there have been attempts on the part of the government still further to extend the number of those groups of government employees who come entirely outside of the civil service. I have under my hand a list of such exemptions. It has been placed on the record repeatedly and I do not think it is necessary to do so again, but it shows clearly that this is by no means a departure but seems to be a part of the policy of the government. The minister said very mildly that he believes the object to be attained is more than slavish maintenance of a

National Revenue Act
principle. If I made such a statement as that I am quite sure that many hon. gentlemen would rise and quite rightly to object to such a dangerous doctrine. Slavish maintenance of a principle! Some of us are inclined to think that we must stand by our principles and that the government ought to stand by its principles, if it has any, in such a case as this. The trouble is that this is throwing the door wide open to expediency of every description; if this can be done in one case it can be done in others, as the minister himself has admitted. He says:	If this particular thing can be better done in this way, by all means let us choose this way. That doctrine could be applied to-day in every department of the government service. We are told with regard to one particular matter: Oh, well, this is a very high appointment; we ought not to trust it to the hands of the Civil Service Commission; it is too technical a service; it is too exalted a position; it must be decided by the government itself. Then the next thing that comes up is the question of digging mud in the banks of the Rideau canal, and we are told that this is an exception; that really no board could determine whether or not men are fitted to dig mud, to dig ditches, and that appointments must be made by the government. So in regard to department after department, the same argument is applied. I mention again this dangerous statement of the minister: "The object to be attained is more important than a slavish maintenance of a principle". That is a very fair statement of the position of the government in this case.
There is one other statement that the minister made, that I should like to repeat. He made this also in such a very moderate way that it sounded very well in the house. I am not quite so sure that it will-I was going to say "sound well" in print, but I had better put it, I am not so sure that it will appear to quite such advantage in print. He said:
It is of vital importance that there should be an efficient appraisal staff.
It seems to me that the minister in making such a statement as that is in reality indicting the Civil Service Commission. If the Civil Service Commission are not in a position to make appointments that are efficient, then I say let us get rid of the present commission, because I quite frankly confess that it is quite possible that the personnel of the Civil Service Commission leaves much to be desired.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is quite possible, and the government has that matter in their own hands. But the way to secure reforms is not to set aside the principle that is behind the establishment of the Civil Service Commission. The way is open to the government to deal with the Civil Service Commission itself. That is what I should like to emphasize. It may be that around the Civil Service Commission there has grown up a certain kind of patronage. We hear that about the corridors, and it may be quite true. It may be that there is favouritism shown by the Civil Service Commission, and there might very well be an investigation held in connection with such matters, because these charges are heard in so many quarters that probably there is some basis for them. I say, let the government investigate the work of the civil service commissioners, their methods and so forth, but let us not set aside the principle underlying the Civil Service Commission.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre ha3 presented the case for the maintenance of the principle of competitive examination and of freedom from patronage in such a clear and able fashion that I do not think it is necessary for any of us to say very much more along that line. As far as my own part of Canada is concerned, we are absolutely opposed to breaking down the idea behind the Civil Service Commission-absolutely opposed. The Free Press has been quoted; the Tribune might also have been quoted. These, I take it, are fair expositions of the general attitude of the people in my own city and throughout the west.
As far as the employees of the Dominion government are concerned, I have had a number of communications from various parts of the country and from different organizations. I shall content myself with reading one, which I think is fairly typical of all. It is one coming from my own city of Winnipeg, and from an organization that is closely affected by the changes proposed in this bill. It is from the Manitoba Customs and Excise Officers' Association, signed by the secretary, and reads::
Reference resolution fifteen March thirtieth now before parliament dealing with certain amendments to the National Revenue Act. Manitoba customs excise officers' association wish to go on record as being opposed to any departure from the present system of appointment and promotion by merit in the civil service. We are of the opinion that the passing of this resolution would be detrimental to the efficiency of the service by removing the incentive of promotion, and because there is no safeguard in the resolution that appointments and promotions would be made to qualified appointees. We are unalterably opposed to anything that, might leave an opening for the return of patronage in the civil service. Kindly take up with all Manitoba members with request for support.
National Revenue Act

I would simply in these few words add my protest against that movement which seems to be growing at the present time to disregard the principle underlying our Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think that this
marks the minister's retreat from the high standard which he has taken in the past in regard to governmental matters. Some members of the cabinet have openly confessed that they retreated long ago, and that they have adopted the principle of destruction of the civil service commission. But in this case the Minister of National Revenue tries to hide his retreat behind the declaration that he does not want to appoint anybody. He says that the minister will not appoint; that the governor in council will appoint. Now when he retires within the secret council chamber, what will be the conditions there? He will ask the Minister of Immigration to appoint an appraiser of silk goods. He will ask the Minister of Agriculture to recommend the appointment of an appraiser in Paris hats and costumes. He will ask the Prime Minister possibly to appoint an appraiser in knitted goods, or silks, or stockings, or something of that kind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: On what does my hon. friend base a statement of that kind, that any individual member of the cabinet will be asked to make a recommendation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am putting it in that way so that the minister will see the ridiculous position in which he is placing himself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is putting himself in a ridiculous position.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The suggestion is
ridiculous, of course, because nobody but the minister himself will make the recommendation. Then why resort to the camouflage of saying that the governor in council will do it? It is the minister himself, and no one else, who will make the recommendations. If he did not, he would have to resort to the ridiculous procedure I suggest, such as asking the Minister of National Defence to recommend an appraiser for musical instruments, or the Minister of Justice to recommend an appraiser for oriental rugs, and so forth. The thing is so ridiculous that one must laugh at the minister, and wonder if he can really believe that the members of the House of Commons are so innocent as to accept his statement.
Passing from that, because I recognize that it is the minister's retreat that is shown in

his acceptance of this bill, I would ask that in his retreat he will nevertheless boldly stand out for the returned soldier, and see that he is placed in the same position in which he stands under the Civil Service Act. I ask him now in his retreat simply to see that an amendment to that effect is placed in this bill before it receives its third reading.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister has made his position perfectly clear in regard to returned soldiers, that he will not include in this bill a provision such as is contained in the Civil Service Act giving a preference to returned men.
There is another matter which it seems to me should be taken care of in this bill, and that is the preference that is given under subsection 3 of section 21 of the Civil Service Act to residents of localities where the appointments are to be made. That subsection reads as follows:
Except as to appointments to positions in the headquarters of the several departments and other portions of the civil service at Ottawa, the appointments to any local positions in any province shall, so far as practicable, be made from bona fide residents of such locality.
I remember when that provision was put in the Civil Service Act. As a matter of fact, I myself moved that this particular provision be inserted and was responsible for having it embodied in the act, and my reason for doing so was that we had found that men and women from other provinces were being brought into British Columbia to fill civil service positions there. That was most objectionable because we considered that we had in the west people who were quite capable of filling these positions, and I remember giving certain instances at that time of appointments which had then recently been made. It seems to me that that principle is being departed from in this case. It is a principle that I think should be preserved in this bill. I believe that, so far as practicable, appointments should be made from among the residents of the locality where the vacancy occurs. I would ask the minister if he is willing to consider an amendment to his bill to take care of that principle.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would say in reply to my hon. friend that the whole purpose of the department in this bill is to try to secure the most capable men for these positions. If it should be found necessary in carrying out that intention to take a man from one part of the country and put him in a position in another part, if I thought that the interests of the service would best be served by so doing, I would have no hesitation in making

National Revenue Act
such an appointment. I should hope that ordinarily men would be taken pretty generally from the district in which they live, and in all probability it would be so done in the great majority of cases; but I do not desire to lay down an absolute rule which would merely destroy the purpose of the bill.
Would the minister embody in his bill subsection 3 of section 21 of the Civil Service Act?
No.

Subsection 4 of section 1 provides that:
The minister may, after such examination as he may prescribe, select and nominate suitable persons for appointment,-
And so on. I understood the minister to say that in the regulations to be prescribed he intends to have the board of appraisers conduct the examination of candidates. If s'o, why not substitute for "such examination as he may prescribe" the words "examination by the board of Dominion appraisers"? If he intends to put this in the regulations, I do not see why he should not embody it in the bill.

Ordinarily we should not attempt to clutter up a bill with what might much better be dealt with by way of regulations; otherwise statutes would be burdened with a great deal of unnecessary matter. But I presume what is in my hon. friend's mind is that the recommendation should go direct from the board of appraisers to the Civil Service Commission in order to avoid what he fears, that the minister himself might exercise political patronage. Am I correct?
It would certainly exclude any supposition of that kind.

My answer is this. The purpose he desires to serve would not be served by inserting in the statute the words suggested, for the simple reason that the members of the board of appraisers are appointed by the minister. If he desired to use his power in a wrongful way, he could use it just as easily through the board of appraisers as in any other manner.
Surely if the board of appraisers recommended certain candidates, and the minister did not want them, he would not go to the extent of dismissing the board.
No.

On several occasions, Mr. Chairman, the minister has stated that it is not his intention to exercise political patronage-to give jobs as rewards for political
services. I do not imagine it is his intention; I never did. But at the same time the house is putting him in the position under this bill of being the one who shall determine what candidates shall be appointed. For instance, the Civil Service Commission may not appoint the person named by the minister in the first place. Then of course there is what the minister terms an additional safeguard; if the appointment is not made by the commission it is made by the governor in council. But there is no use for any of us to think that the governor in council will cadi candidates and examine them. It is simply a question of accepting or not accepting the minister's recommendation; and he has stated that they will accept his recommendation. Undoubtedly this constitutes patronage, in that it gives him power, as head of the department, to make appointments. The burden of his argument is that he needs qualified appraisers. If that argument is sound, 1 may point out that a similar argument has been used in connection with the preventive service, and to-day the minister stated that he intended to put the preventive service back under the Civil Service Commission.
No. I stated that appointments to the special preventive service, now entirely under the minister, would be made in exactly the same way as appointments of appraisers.

The member for Bow
River (Mr. Garland) on April 23 inquired of the ministry with regard to the preventive service. That return has not yet been brought down, although it passed the house some time ago. Whatever may be said with regard to statements made by the minister and other members of the government when they were in opposition, I think it is easy to demonstrate by referring to the debates of this house that all ministries handle patronage appointments in a way that they would not readily admit should be handled by the representatives of another party if it was in power. That seems to be the general attitude. Most of the declarations read this afternoon were made by members now sitting to the right of the Speaker when they were in opposition.
I think it will be generally conceded that not only the people, but civil servants themselves, are afraid of patronage. In the abstract, patronage has been condemned by everyone except those who for the time being have been handling it. I have before me two telegrams that were sent to my desk-mate (Mr. Garland). He is not in the house this
National Revenue Act

afternoon or doubtless he would be reading them himself. The first telegram is as follows:
E. J. Garland,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Understand resolutions before parliament affecting appointments and promotions in Department of National Revenue. This association believes appointments and promotions under Civil Service Commission as at present preferable to anything savouring of return to patronage, and beg that you use your influence accordingly.
George Edgecombe,
Secretary,
Northern Alberta Customs and Excise Officers Association.
The other message is from Quebec:
E. J. Garland, M.P.
With reference to proposed amendment to National Revenue Act introduced by honourable Minister National Revenue, we respectfully submit that if resolution is carried in its original form the very object which the Civil Service Act nineteen eighteen had in view would be defeated; and we respectfully draw your attention to the fact that if said resolution is pressed in house same should be strenuously opposed, because if carried would simply mean a return to patronage, a state of affairs which we believe to be detrimental to the service, as it would deprive an officer of incentive in the way of promotion and tend to lessen the morale of the service and impair its efficiency.
Quebec Customs and Excise Officers Association.
J. A. Young, President.
W. P. Fitzpatrick, Secretary.
There is no question, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is asking for power that in the hands of his successor might be used to set up a system of patronage in the department. The minister is quite emphatic in his refusal to consider any amendments regarding returned soldiers or tending otherwise to restrict the power under this bill to determine who shall be appointed to the positions dealt with. For that reason I am opposed to the bill. Of course the minister may be quite confident that he has the necessary majority to vote the bill through anyway. But we have taken a stand against anything of this sort in days gone by, and I think it is only proper that we should stand by the Civil Service Commission until we can see it demonstrated, by reference to past experience, that it has been better for the civil service and for the revenues of the country that civil servants should be appointed on any other principle than the merit system. Of course, it is easy to show that mistakes have been made in the past under the merit system. No system is perfect. But after all we are dealing with fMr. Kennedy.]
patronage versus the merit system, and I do not think there is anyone to-day, in a responsible position, who will stand up and defend patronage as against the merit system.

I decline to be put in the
position of appearing to be opposed to any preference being given the returned men, or of desiring the abolition of the merit system. I want to say emphatically that such an attitude is entirely foreign to my intention. It is merely a question of embodying an amendment in the act, and I do not see how any such amendments as my hon. friends suggest, incorporated in the act, would ensure against a minister who deliberately desired to exercise discrimination either against men already in the service or against returned men.
The bill gives the minister power to ignore the commission.

I do not propose to
trespass long on the time of the committee, but I do submit that the minister has approached the matter from the wrong standpoint. He has endeavoured to make an exception to the rule: what he should endeavour to do is to bring all appointments within the rule. That is what he should be labouring to accomplish to-day instead of seeking to discover exceptions to the rule. I find that when the Spinney bill was considered by parliament it was based upon a report submitted by a select committee, of which the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) was a member; and in making a speech on that occasion in reference to the report, the hon. gentleman said:
Technical, professional and scientific employees, it was generally felt, should be appointed with the advice of the deputy heads of the departments.
It is for that principle that we on this side of the house contend; that is to say, that technical and professional men should be appointed with the assistance of deputy heads of the departments. But the appointing power should be with the Civil Service Commission. Any departure from that principle is wrong, and in this instance the minister is departing from it, although he is endeavouring, by a clever use of words in his bill, to utilize the Civil Service Commission in order to give an air, shall we say, of fairness to proposals that are purely political.
Now, we are not dealing with the minister himself, if he will only bear that in mind. We are not dealing with the hon. gentleman personally, but with the Minister of National Revenue, in relation to the question of ap-

National Revenue Act
pointing professional or technical men with the assistance of deputy heads of departments. That is the subject matter of the discussion. We desire efficiency in the public service. How shall that efficiency be secured? It has been decided by this parliament times without number-and in very many instances owing to the urgings of members who now sit opposite-that the Civil Service Commission provides means whereby efficiency may be secured without recourse to political patronage. That is the principle underlying the Civil Service Act. A departure from that principle is now proposed. That departure, the minister says, is an exception to the rule. But we submit that the method by which the position of the civil service can best be maintained is a simple one: all you have to do is to ask the board of appraisers to set the examination and let the candidates write them as they please. Let the Civil Service Commission conduct the examinations, so far as responsibility for them is concerned, and make the appointments, giving the preference, as the Civil Service Act provides, to returned soldiers. Is it beyond the reach of the Civil Service Commission to get a gentleman from Montreal who was an assistant buyer in a great departmental store to be an appraiser of leather values? Is it impossible for the commission to get one who had been for six or seven years in a trust company, and who in years gone by was associated with the textile industry, to be an appraiser of the products of that industry? Could not the Civil Service Commission do that as well as the minister and his commissioner? The question is a simple one. If the Civil Service Commission is to function, and parliament intends that it shall make the appointments, let the board of appraisers set the examinations and have the commission assume responsibility for them and for the appointments.
As regards the second question-giving preference to returned men-this is a principle in the Civil Service Act which, we contend, should be maintained. If maintained in its integrity it would have the result of retaining in Canada a large number of returned men who are now in another country. All you need to do is to ask for the returns and you will find hOw many Canadians are receiving pensions in the republic to the south of us and who should be getting them in Canada.
Under these circumstances, so far as we on this side are concerned, the minister may take his bill out of committee, and on the third reading we will offer the two amendments to which I have referred. On the third reading it will be recorded whether or not
this house proposes to revert to the old system of patronage which in practice has been so disastrous to this country, and to take from men who have deserving claims on the country the preference which the Civil Service Act now gives them.

My purpose is to get the best men available.

If they are equally qualified they will receive the preference.

The house resumed from May 14 consideration in committee of Bill No. 289, to amend the Pension Act-Mr. King (Kootenay)-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 5-Commission attached to department.

When the committee rose we were dealing with sections 5 and 30; it was suggested that these sections stand for further consideration. I have given the matter some thought, and I think the section as drawn is quite proper and does not in any way curtail the activities of the Board of Pension Commissioners; in fact, it places in the statute the conditions under which we are operating to-day. In 1920 the government of the day brought into the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment those officers who were formerly attached to the pension board; the only mistake they made at that time was to make the medical officers and investigators departmental officers. As I explained to the house, it is my purpose to leave with the commission those officers upon whom they must depend for information on which to base their judgments, and these are principally the medical officers and investigators. These officers will be under the control of the pension board and will report directly to that body. The other officers, the clerks, stenographers and other employees of that kind, will be in the office of the commission but will be employed by the department. I now move that subsection 4 of section 5 be amended by striking out the words "for the purposes of the department", in the fifth line.

I have one or two remarks
to make in connection with section 5. In order to function quite properly and to the satisfaction of those with whom it has to deal, the Board of Pension Commissioners should be a body within itself and should not be controlled by any other body, least of all by any department of the government. Thus far we have had an independent Board of Pension Commissioners. Of course objections have been taken to some of the rulings of that board, and officials who have to deal with applications for pension, as in the case of other applications for relief, are not always as popular as they might be. However, I think perhaps we might say that some of this unpopularity, if such there be, has been caused through the fact that the board stands up so straight that it leans backward. I

think it cannot be accused with cause of consciously exercising favouritism or discrimination.
The orders in council to which the minister referred were passed in 1920 and 1921, and authorized the transfer of certain officers of the board to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I think the minister is right, as far as my information goes, when he states that practically all the officers were transferred with the exception of secretaries and the medical advisers. However, the minister must be aware of the fact that this did not work out well and was the cause of an increasing dissatisfaction which culminated in the investigation conducted by Mr. Scott of Montreal into the working of the department. Mr. Scott made his report in October of 1927; certain contentions of the board were before him and probably formed the basis for his investigation and finding. It was alleged, and I think upheld by Mr. Scott, that opinion and advice was deliberately given by departmental officials to applicants for pension, and in many cases this advice was erroneous. Contrary to the provisions of the statute, pensions were diverted by the department, without the consent of the board, in order to recover departmental outlays and expenditures for hospital maintenance, medical attention and so on, and I think I am right in saying that diversions were made to reimburse certain advances made from the disablement fund. These matters were gone into, and Mr. Scott recommended inter alia as follows:
(1) The Board of Pension Commissioners should be given such staff or medical examiners, investigators, and clerks as will enable them to function as an independent body for the purpose of,-
(a) Collecting all necessary information and evidence relating to matters relevant to the eligibility of ex-service men and their dependents for pensions, rendering decisions thereon, and calculating the pensions payable.
I submit to the minister that his proposed bill does not give effect to this recommendation; in other words, it perpetuates the very evil which Mr. Scott found to be more or less rampant in the administration of the department. The commission is no longer nominally possessed of the independence which it formerly had, and it is now definitely attached to the department. The bill says in terms, "The commission shall be attached to the department." I do not know what that means, but certainly it is open to the interpretation that the board is now under the department in exercising some of the functions which it must exercise.

Pension Act
Mr. KING (Kootenay). Section 6 of the original act did the same thing.

I have not bothered to read the whole section, but it is as follows.
The commission shall be attached to the department and the expenses required to be incurred for the discharge of its duties, including the salaries of its officers, clerks, and other employees shall be met out of the moneys provided by parliament for the purposes of the department.
I submit that this is an entirely different kind of attachment from that which existed heretofore and the tendency, if not the fact, is to remove the independence of the tribunal which has been set up and to make that tribunal more or less subservient to the control of the department which is a part of the government; in that way pensions will be brought into politics. If there is one thing on which I think I can speak for the men of the forces, one thing in which they are vitally interested, it is that pensions never should get into politics; pensions must be kept out of politics and there must be a feeling among the men that everyone is being treated on his merits, with no bias, no discrimination and no favouritism. I do submit to the minister that this section is inclined to place this important department under and attached to the new Department of Pensions and National Health, and in fact strikes a blow at the independence heretofore enjoyed by that board.
As I understand it, the appropriation for the board is now voted by parliament; we have the say as to what money they may spend, and having that say we can also control how they spend it. Now it is proposed to do away with the appropriation for the board; under this act it will be transferred to the department, and the staff at present under the control of the board will be placed on the departmental pay roll. I submit that that is an evasion; it is not good, and it is not conducive to the proper determination of applications. It does not give the men the independent tribunal to which they are entitled. I think it follows that the board will be entirely in the hands of the department, as to what staff it may have, and what staff is to be loaned to the board by the department. That is a most important matter. They should not be limited to the staff that the Department of Pensions and National Health chooses to let them have. The Department of Pensions and National Health may let the board have only such staff as will do the work the department wants it to do, and no more; that is, the board may not be allowed to have a sufficient or properly appointed staff.
Then, there is no provision made for an annual report, as it will be absorbed in the report of the Department of Pensions and National Health. I submit that the whole status of the board will become that of a commission within the department. It will not be a commission outside the department, a commission standing on its own feet, and functioning independently-it has no allowance by this government in the way of funds- but it will be a commission of some sort or other within the department. No one has been able to convince me, and I have discussed this matter, that it will not tend towards the board gradually coming under the dominance of the department, and so pensions will be put in politics. I do not know whether I understood the minister to say that the status as a deputy head is to be cancelled.

It is not usual
in a case of this kind.

It is not usual, but it has
worked out very well; it should have the status of a deputy head of a department.
I think the minister will agree with me that the commission's power will be curtailed to that of merely giving decisions upon medical examinations and investigations, on reports not obtained by itself, but obtained and made by officials over whom it has no direction or control; officials of the Department of Pensions and National Health. That is a decided change. In speaking of this Pension Act, the minister has said, as appears on page 2571 of Hansard:
The pension commission will remain as they are at present, independent, but it is true that this department, in the course of its administrative work, vdll pay the cheques after the adjudication has been made.
I submit that this bill, as it is brought down, is not in accordance with that statement. I do not say that the minister has ignored that in drafting this section, but I do think that if he considers the objections I have raised-just to give him something to reply to; we will discuss it more in detail as time goes on-he will find that the whole trend of this section is to destroy that independence which is so precious, and which should not be touched in the slightest degree. I think he will come to the conclusion that he has gone too far in this bill, and that the power of the commissioners has been seriously interfered with. It is quite likely that it will become a mere adjunct politically, instead of an outstanding independent body.
I submit that the matter is of the highest importance to the men, women and children who are concerned with pensions, and this section should not be passed without the very
Pension Act

closest scrutiny and consideration. I bespeak the co-operation of the minister in giving sympathetic consideration to what has been said. I do not want him to feel that he has to stick to something that he has done, but I ask him to keep an open mind so that as the discussion proceeds and he finds possibly that we are right he may be prepared to modify the section to meet our views. I speak for what I consider the best interests of the soldiers, some at least of whom feel very much alarmed about this section. I do not want him to shake his head at this moment, because the discussion will probably go on for some time, and I hope he will see the light before we are finished.

I think my hon. friend is labouring under a misapprehension. If he will read the old section and then the new one he will find that we have tried to embody in the latter what was covered by three or four sections heretofore. As far as the commission is concerned, it is an independent body; we have nothing to do, and will have nothing to do, with its adjudication or consideration of pension cases. All we propose to do, under this amendment, is just what we have been doing heretofore, with the exception of a small personal staff of clerks and stenographers here in Ottawa. I cannot conceive why the payment and auditing of those salaries should not be done in one department rather than in two and that that is all that is intended by this amendment.
In regard to the medical staff required for investigations and examinations, I think the commission should have this staff and, in fact, it has been the practice in the department since the Scott report. These officers are now under the immediate direction of the board and if it requires any officers of ours at any time it merely makes the request, and the officers become all officers of the Pension department and report to the pension board.
I am sure there is no desire on the part of the government, and it certainly is not my desire, to encroach in any way upon the pension board, or to interfere with its independence. It has been the desire of parliament since its inception that such a thing should not occur, and I am satisfied that desire still exists. In the administration I believe a great saving could be made and overlapping prevented. I cannot see where the making out of the cheques in the department will in any way interfere with the activities of the commission, or with its independence.
At one time the pension board had some four or five hundred employees scattered

throughout Canada. In 1920 the government of that date did not hesitate, by order in council, to strip the board of those employees, leaving only a small group here at Ottawa. As I said before, I think probably a mistake was made at that time when they did not leave the medical officers within the control of the pension board. The section does not materially affect the administration as it has been carried on in the past, and will not affect the independence of the pension board.

Subject to the provisions of this act, and of any regulations made under the provisions of this act. the commission shall have full power and authority to deal with all matters pertaining to pensions, consider all applications for pension, and to award, refuse, cancel, pay and administer pensions.

Bell Telephone Company

The object of this bill, Mr. Chairman, is to raise the capital of the company from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000. The company operates in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. This is the part of our country which is the most densely populated; the telephone service in that territory is expanding from day to day and in a proportion much greater than the growth of the population. The increase in the demand for additional telephone service comes from the cities and from the rural parts of the country. The farmers all want to be able to communicate quickly one with the other and with the cities and towns where they market their products.
This expansion necessarily involves large expenditures every year and the capital to provide for these outlays can only be obtained in two ways, by borrowings and by the issue of additional capital. Expanding continuously from year to year the company must get its funds on the money markets, whatever may happen to be the conditions of these markets at the time. To do this successfully, it must be careful to maintain its credit at a very high level. That is for it the thing of paramount importance, the maintenance of its credit. Its borrowings, therefore, must remain within a very conservative margin of its physical assets. If the company exceeded that limit, and thus impaired its credit, the public would be the first to suffer by it.
The only other source of funds is the issue of capital. The company, having practically exhausted its present authorized capital, and having to meet the demands of the public for additional service, must therefore be authorized to increase its capital.
The increase asked for may at first sight be deemed excessive, but a short examination of the records of the company and of its present situation should convince any unprejudiced mind that the amount is not exorbitant. It is calculated to provide for the needs of the company during the next ten years.
The last increase in capital took place in 1920, and it was for $45,000,000. During these eight years that amount was subscribed by the public at par, or above par, and was invested in the plant; it provided for the natural development of the operations of the company. There is no complaint at all about the use which was made of that money. This amount was not the only investment in additions and extensions to the plant. In 1920 the bonded indebtedness of the company was $16,750,000. That was raised by $23,250,000 to $40,000,000, so that the total capital expenditures on additional plant and equipment 
amounted to $68,000,000, apart altogether from investments of the depreciation fund.
The average increase in telephones during these years was 38,000 per year. Last year the capital expenditures of the company amounted to $18/100,000; the construction program of the company for the next five years calls for capital expenditures of 102 million dollars. Under such conditions the increase asked for seems to be normal and justified.
A refusal to pass this bill would mean that parliament would intervene to prevent the company from providing the additional telephone facilities demanded by the public. This is a public utility company; it is compelled by its charter to extend the service to whoever asks for it if he complies with certain conditions. After having put this obligation upon the company should this house refuse it the right to issue the additional capital which it requires for that very purpose, it would be a most unfair situation, and as a representative of the province of Quebec I protest against such a stand.

On section 1-Incorporation.

When this bill was before the committee last I had spoken for four or five minutes, and stated that this bill should not be allowed to pass. Governor Smith of the state of New York has taken the stand that such international bridges should be built by the state or federal authority or by the municipal authority, and this parliament has 36103-193
jurisdiction over bridges which are international or interprovincia! or which affect navigation. In this connection I would like to quote the words of Governor Smith:
Such bridges should be built by the state or states or by one more governmental subdivisions or by a public municipal authority similar to the port authority," the governor declared in his blanket veto of the three measures. "If such a bridge is to be built over international waters it should be constructed jointly by the United States in conjunction with the Canadian government or by the state of New York in conjunction with the Canadian province affected."
Such projects, the governor felt could be financed at lower cost by the state or federal governments, while, he added, "they are in their very nature public; to authorize privately-owned toll bridges is a step as backward as to authorize privately-owned highways, under the wording of these acts, the franchise is practically made perpetual."
"If it pays private corporations to erect these bridges," the governor's memorandum continued, "it will certainly pay the state to do it. If tolls are to be charged, the state should be the recipient of the tolls, and they should not be in excess of what is required to operate and maintain property, pay the interest on the bonds and make the necessary annual contributions to the sinking fund for their retirement."
I contend that since this public policy has been laid down by the governor of the state of New York we should not pass this bill tonight. In addition to that we must remember that there is considerable dispute with regard to the rights of navigation in this case; which should be paramount in any event over the interests of anyone's private bill. This is contested international territory running from Brockville through Cornwall to the great port of Montreal. The rights of navigation are paramount. This is an international stream, and it is contended that it is subject to the rights of navigation. The surplus waters belong to the province subject to navigation and the bed of the river, the banks and rapids.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, this question should not be considered at the present time, until the decision has been given by the Supreme Court of Canada, as referred to in sessional papers No. 50, P.C. 115, dated January 18th, 1928. As this is an international question, affecting both countries, I cannot understand why there should not be a special sitting of the supreme court to hear and determine this question and not lay it over until the fall. The delays are not at all creditable. The provinces of Quebec and Ontario and the government of Canada will be represented by counsel on this hearing, and no matter what the decision is regarding
