One of the matters involved is this particular question of the erection of bridges and other erections on international streams affecting navigation. These various questions have come up for a decision by the supreme court, because of the order in council to which I referred, and which reads as follows:
Does the ownership by the province of the bed of any stream, whether such bed be level or sloping, give to the province the ownership of water powers:
(a)	created thereupon by Dominion works for the improvement of navigation; or
(b)	existing thereupon by nature?
Clause 2 of the reference covers the particular bill now before the chair. Clause 3 reads as follows:
Has the province any proprietary interest in or legislative control over:
(a) the canals, with lands and water power connected therewith, and the lake and river improvements which were conveyed to the Dominion by section 108, schedule 3, of the British North America Act, 1867, or in or over the disposal of any water powers created thereby or existing thereupon from time to time; or
This particular bridge will extend from the province of Ontario over to the state of New York, and it is covered by the four comers of this particular reference. The clause continues:
_ (b) water-powers created by works for the improvement of navigation constructed by or under the authority of the Dominion since confederation; or
(c)	works constructed wholly for power purposes by the Dominion out of moneys appropriated by parliament for such purpose?
All of these subsections have to be read together, regarding the erection over international streams of public works, of bridges or similar structures, and an application is further necessary under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. The fourth clause of this particular reference also covers this bridge, and reads as follows:
Has the Dominion exclusive legislative power to regulate waters for the purpose of navigation:
(a)	in navigable waters; and
(b)	in non-navigable waters?
This particular river is navigable right at this point. If this erection is allowed by an order in council of this government, or is allowed after a proper hearing with all parties present, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act such an erection will come within the four corners of this clause. Another reason why the bridge is within the reference is because of clause 5, which reads as follows:

Where the Dominion, for navigation purposes, expropriates or uses any part of the bed of any stream vested in the province, is the province entitled to any compensation for such expropriation or use?
Then clauses 6 and 7 read as follows:
6.	Has the Dominion the exclusive legislative control over and proprietary interest in water-powers brought into being by works authorized by parliament to be erected in an international stream for the purpose of carrying out an agreement between Canada and any foreign country looking to the erection of joint works for the improvement of navigation in such stream? If not, what are the powers and rights of the province with regard to such water-powers?
7.	Where the bed of a navigable stream is owned by the province or by a private individual, is the title of such owner subordinate to the public right of navigation, and to the provision of any statute which may be enacted from time to time by parliament, within the powers conferred by section 91 (10) of the British North America Act, 1867.
This particular reference of a public matter affects the body politic of Canada. This matter is now before the Supreme Court of Canada on a reference, and is sub judice and this parliament should not forestall what action the Supreme Court of Canada would take in that particular case regarding the right to cross this navigable stream to the state of New York by a private bridge. The rights of navigation are paramount, and a structure cannot be erected there without joint consent of Canada and the state of New York. I contend that it is against public policy; it is contrary to public policy that private parties % should be given extraordinary powers such as this legislation proposes to give.
Well, the bill goes to the foot of the list, and it will not do any harm if it never gets up again.

I do not want to get into an argument over this. On section 25-No pension to widow unless married before disability, or living with or maintained by pensioner.

I am very glad that the minister of this department and the Minister of National Defence and the chairman of the pensions committee are so broad in their views in regard to this act, and that we may introduce matters other than those considered by the committee if it appears that something has been omitted.
I have two suggestions to offer in regard to section 25. The first is in the nature of a legal amendment, and the other one affects the principle of the act.
Taking first the legal amendment, I submit that this section can have no effect as it stands. Paragraph (b) (i) reads:
Provided that a pension shall be paid when a member of the forces on and after the coming into force of this act secures from the commission a certificate showing that any pensionable injury or disease from which he was suffering at the time of the marriage would not in the opinion of the commission result in death.
The intention of the committee I know was that the words "on and after the coming into force of this act" should mean the coming into effect of this amendment, whereas if the section is passed in its present form it becomes a part of the principal act and will be read as a part of that act, and the words "on and after the coming into force of this act" will mean the 7th of July, 1919, the date on which the principal act came into effect. I do not want to elaborate on this argument. There are decisions of the courts on the point, but unless it is necessary-

That question has been submitted to the Department of Justice, and their report is in accordance with the view of my hon. friend, that we should substitute

the words "on and after July 1, 1988," for the words "on and after the coming into force of this act."

Before the section is agreed to I wish to bring to the minister's attention something else which I think is very serious. As an illustration, take the case of many soldiers who returned, say, in 1918, before the passing of the main Pensions Act, and who married after their return, probably as the result of an engagement made prior to the war, in ignorance of the provision that the widow would not be entitled to a pension if she married a disabled soldier after the appearance of the disability; in fact she probably married him when he was apparently quite fit and without any expectation of death as a result of the disability. How is that case provided for under these amendments? Take subsection (i).

Subsection (i) applies
to future marriages. Subsections (ii) and (iv) are applicable.

Subsection (ii) provides:
That a pension shall be paid in the case of a member of the forces who has married before the coming into force of this act, and who has obtained from the commission a certificate showing that any pensionable injury or disease from which he was suffering at the time of the marriage, would not in the opinion of the commission result in death.

Pension Act
Nearly ten years have elapsed, and I should say that hundreds of these men have died as a result of the disability referred to, and their widows are not receiving a pension. How can you provide for such cases under that subsection? Obviously they are not provided for, and those men who married in 1919, before this act came into force, are surely the most deserving of all, for they married in ignorance of any prohibitive provisions. Now take subsection (iii) :
That a pension shall be paid in the case of a member of the forces who has married and who has died of a pensionable disability prior to the coming into force of this act,-
Perhaps this is the clause which is intended to apply:
-if, at the time of the marriage, the condition of such member of the forces was such that the prospective wife after making reasonable enquiries would not anticipate that the injury or disease would be a substantial factor in causing death, provided, however, that it shall be conclusively presumed that such injury or disease was not a substantial factor in causing death, if at the time of the marriage there existed no resultant pensionable disability from such injury or disease.
Just picture a woman who married a returned soldier in 1918 now proving that she made reasonable inquiries which led her not to anticipate that the injury would result in death. Why would she make " reasonable inquiries " as to the expectation of the man's life? I think the suggestion really is not fair. It is rather ridiculous to expect that the wife would make such inquiries, for there was nothing in the law at the time to make it necessary for her to do so. That argument might be used after the main Pensions Act came into effect, when she would be warned that if she married after the appearance of the disability she would get no pension; but for those cases where marriage took place before the passing of the main Pensions Act it is not reasonable. Now subsection (iv):
That a pension shall be paid in the case of a member of the forces who has married prior to the coining into force of this act and who fails to apply to the commission for a certificate showing that any pensionable injury or disease from which he was suffering at the time of the marriage would not in the opinion of the commission result in death and who subsequently dies of a pensionable disability if at the time of the marriage the condition of such member of the forces was such that the prospective wife after making reasonable enquiries would not anticipate that the injury or disease would be a substantial factor in causing death; provided, however, that it shall be conclusively presumed that such injury or disease was not a substantial factor in causing death, if at the time of the marriage, there existed no resultant pensionable disability from such injury or disease.
The same argument applies to this subsection. I would make two suggestions. First, that we adopt the provision which was embodied in Bill No. 70 in 1925 which passed this house, and which provided:
That a pension shall be paid when the marriage takes place prior to a date one year after discharge of a member of the forces.
That would cover the cases I have mentioned of men who married before the coming into effect of the main Pensions Act, and would give them a year after their discharge within which to complete the contract of marriage and protect the wife. The other suggestion is that the words:
-or if the member of the forces was not in receipt of a pension at the time of the marriage.
-be added at the end of paragraphs (iii) and (iv). Then the last sentence in each paragraph would read:
-provided, however, that it shall be conclusively presumed that such injury or disease was not a substantial factor in causing death, if at the time of the marriage there existed no resultant pensionable disability from such injury or disease, or if the member of the forces was not in receipt of a pension at the time of the marriage.
It would have this effect. As it stands now, if there is a pensionable disability for which the man has not been pensioned, the widow is out of luck and can never receive a pension. It seems to me that the words " or if the member of the forces was not in receipt of a pension at the time of the marriage" ought to be conclusive and the wife should be entitled to a pension should he die as a result of this disability. This section is a very complicated one and requires some mature consideration on the part of the minister and of the law officers of the crown. The section should stand until the minister has had a chance to reconsider it. I firmly believe that there are two or three points in it which have escaped the attention of the committee and which ought to be reconsidered before the section passes.

As regards the case where marriage was solemnized soon after the termination of the war, or soon after discharge, the sections as drafted are, I think, intended to cover every case. The section to which my hon. friend refers, embodied in the bill of 1925, is now covered by the sections before us. What the 1925 bill did was to make it absolutely sure that where a woman married within a year after discharge, in the event of the death of her husband she would be entitled to pension if there was a total or a pensionable disability. Now it depends on what seems to be the really logical factor in
Pension Act

deciding these cases. My hon. friend knows, as does the house, that the reason for the section as it originally stood was the desire to avoid a repetition of the experience of other countries; so that this country would not be paying pensions in cases where the marriage was, or might be said to have been, a death bed marriage. The result of this practice in the republic to the south of us has been that they are still paying pensions on account of the civil war.
I would point out to the committee that this section is much broader than the provisions in England. In England, if the marriage took place after the discharge of the soldier or after the end of the war, no pension is payable to the widow if the man dies from a pensionable disability. We are going much further, and I for one am very much pleased indeed to see that we are adopting the principle contained in this section. But the principle is that there must be some examination of the circumstances under which the marriage was performed; and if the marriage was performed under such circumstances that the woman could reasonably anticipate that the injury or disease from which her future husband was suffering at that time-if it happened to be a war disability-would eventually cause his death, then no pension would be paid, inasmuch as it involved a liability not contemplated at the time of enlistment. That is the principle of sections 3 and 4.
There is another provision to the effect that the spouse may make the thing more certain by going to the Board of Pension Commissioners and asking them to inquire into the circumstances of the husband's physical condition at the time of marriage, and give a certificate that at the time of marriage the injury or disability was not of such a nature as, in the opinion of the commission, would result in death. Under either of these circumstances the pension is payable, and in a number of cases I have examined it would appear as if a great many of those who heretofore have been denied pensions will get the benefit of the amendment which is offered. May I say further that the effect of the amendment is not simply to provide for cases where death occurs at some time in the future, but to permit widows who have already made applications, and whose applications have been refused, to come now to the board and say, "We are able to prove the circumstances which are required under these sections and are therefore entitled to pension".
That would be since the act came into force-since 1919.

No; my hon. friend did
not get the effect of the provision.
I read it carefully.

The effect of the first
section is that in the case of all past marriages-
Regardless of time.

Yes, so long as they were before July first, 1928, as now provided by the amendment suggested by my hon. friend from Burrard. So that everyone gets the benefit of it whether the marriage takes place within a year or two years or three.
It is now ten years after the war. I may say to the committee that in the United States, under their pension legislation, the right to pension of the widow of a soldier ceases, as I understand it, ten years after the war. If the marriage takes place any time after ten years subsequent to the war, the right to pension goes. So that we are doing better, because by this act if marriage takes place fifteen years after the war, provided a certificate can be obtained, the widow can still claim pension, I do think the section ought to commend itself to the committee, and in the interests of those whom it is sought to benefit it would be inadvisable to attempt to incorporate in it any arbitrary provisions. We have already tried to deal, under the meritorious clause, with the cases which my hon. friend from Burrard has mentioned. The hon. member probably knows of cases of men who were engaged before they went overseas and who have applied under the meritorious clause, and some cases have been granted.
And some refused.
Would they come under this section?

Yes; look at subsections
(ii) and (iv); they are covered in both. If they are still living they may go to the Board of Pension Commissioners and get a certificate; and it is provided that even if they do not get a certificate and death occurs subsequently the widow may s'till go to the board and say, "At the time I was married to my husband this was his physical condition and I had no reasonable ground for expecting that it would cause his death." In either case the pension is granted, so that the section covers the case mentioned by my hon. friend. The section to which the hon. gentleman has referred did not meet with the response which this country desired, and I hope that this section will have a more favourable response. This is word for word in keeping with the report of the committee, except for the fact that we have substituted July 1 for the words "before the coming into force of this act", and I feel that substantial relief is being afforded.
Pension Act

The minister says that this provision covers the case I have mentioned. I thought I had made it clear that it does not. What woman, before there was a pension law, would make reasonable inquiries as to the expectation of life of her fiance? Yet this is what is required here. The only other provision under which she can secure recognition is this:
Provided, however, that it shall be conclusively presumed that such injury or disease was not a substantial factor in causing death, if at the time of the marriage there existed no resultant pensionable disability from such injury or disease.
But if the pension board, subsequent to the marriage, finds that the man, prior to the marriage, was suffering from a disease which afterwards progressed to such an extent that he became pensionable after marriage- although the disease pre-existed marriage- then under the subsection referred to the woman will not be entitled to pension.

My hon. friend is taking
the proviso the wrong way; it is a proviso for the benefit of the wife, and it states that in certain cases it is conclusively presumed that the disease did not contribute to death. It does not say that in other cases it may not be proved that the disease did not contribute to death. If it comes under this proviso, if it is conclusively presumed, that does not stop her from proving it quite apart from that.
If there is no resultant pensionable disability.
But this does not say that because there was a resultant pensionable disability it is thereby presumed that that disability was going to cause death.

As I said before, this is
very complicated; I see it one way and the minister sees it another. This is how I see it:	If no resultant pensionable disability
existed at the time of marriage the woman may qualify for pension, but if after the marriage it is ascertained that a disability existed prior to the marriage for which he was afterwards pensionable, under that subsection she cannot qualify for a pension.

Under that proviso she
does not get the benefit of that conclusive presumption, but she may show that the disability was not one which would likely cause death.

Now the minister and I are in perfect agreement. Now, show me the woman who, in 1918, before there was a pension law, would think of making reasonable inquiries as to whether or not her fiance had a reasonable expectation of life. No man or woman would ever think of such a thing.

Why does my hon. friend
mention 1918?
I mention it for the reason that many men returned from the front in 1918 and many were married in that year, but the Pension Act did not come into effect until July 1919.
There were pension regulations before that, and there was the old Militia Pension Act.

Yes, but the difference is
this: They would have notice of an law on the statutes, but they would not have notice of any regulations. Ignorance of the regulations might be excused, but ignorance of the Pension Act would not excuse them.

That applies to anybody married up to July 1, 1928, or until to-night, when we are discussing this matter. These people have had no notice of this, but my hon. friend will remember that the situation suggested is whether a prospective wife made reasonable inquiries. Perhaps there were no inquiries necessary, -but I would have thought that if the prospective husband suffered from a severe disability it would be reasonable to assume that the two of them together would consult a doctor as to what effect that disability would have, whether in 1918 or 1929.

No, the minister does not
get my point. In 1919 there was a statute passed, which said they were not entitled to a pension if they married after the appearance of the disability, but they did not know of that in 1918.
Yes, the same provision was there.-
But it was not on the staute books.
Does my hon. friend think either one of the parties read the statutes or the regulations?

There is a difference in the legal position, and that makes their case so much stronger. I feel that the words "or if the member of the forces was not in receipt of a pension at the time of the marriage" should be added at the end of the sections (iii) and (iv). That does not make any very material difference, but it will clear up that point about the resultant pensionable disability. I ask the minister to take that under consideration and not press this section through to-night.
Pension Act

The principle involved in this section always has met with my bitter opposition ever since we have had pension committees. I have supported the principle that any widow who married a soldier after the appearance of his disability was not entitled to pension in case her husband died. That is the opinion held in England as laid down in the statutes of that country, and I have been one of those who fought against the adoption of that principle here. This is the principle which was also adopted by the senate. I would call that fact to the attention of my leader, hoping that some day it might qualify me for a place in the senate. However, this year I allowed myself to be convinced that possibly a good case could be made out for the widow who married after the appearance of the disability.
Does my hon. friend think it would be possible to arrange for a seat in the senate right away, in order to let us get this measure through?
I heartily endorse that suggestion. I do not know whether there are any vacancies from my province just now, but if my hon. friend would help me out we might create one.
My hon. friend can reform the senate then.

Certainly it would be a good senate then. However, I was prepared to accept the principle that in certain cases a widow who marries a man whom she knew to suffer a disability should get a pension; the thought I had in my mind and which was entertained by many others was to get away from the danger of death bed marriages and of perpetual pensions going on for years after the death of the soldier, benefiting people who could not be considered to have helped the soldier in any way while he was at war. The government of this country promised the soldier when he went away that they would look after his dependants, his wife and his children, but they did not promise to look after any wife he might marry after he returned.
I am free to admit that a case has been made out with respect to the returned soldier when we say that if in the event of his death we deprive his widow of a pension, in certain circumstances possibly we deprive him of a chance of getting married, although I do not believe this country would think very much of the woman who would refuse to marry a returned soldier on the ground that she would not be in receipt of a pension in case he died.

However, that principle has been accepted, and I submit to this committee that it should be restricted in every possible way in order that this country may not be burdened for years and generations to come with pensions which have not been earned but which may be paid to people who have no possible right to them. So we are surrounding this measure with certain restrictions.
It was proposed to the committee that persons who could prove a bona fide engagement to marry before the soldier went overseas should be entitled to pension. That contention received strong support from the National Council of Women and from a great many members of the committee, and I think would receive support from the public also. However, it must be remembered that here would be involved the question of evidence of an engagement to marry, which is a very difficult thing to prove. In many cases, the soldier being dead, the only evidence we would have would be that of the person claiming pension, and without saying anything derogatory to the soldier who went overseas, I submit that we would have hundreds of applicants who would come before the Board of Pension Commissioners and produce affidavits to the effect that in 'London they became engaged to marry a certain soldier who was afterwards killed overseas, or who returned to Canada and afterwards died as the result of a disability incurred overseas. I think to have admitted that principle would have made the act unworkable.
Other suggestions were made; it was suggested that in the case of soldiers who married within one year after their discharge and afterwards died the widows should be entitled to pension. I submit that if we place any such time limit it will be extended again and again, as has already happened this year in another connection. So the committee thought it advisable, instead of playing with questions of limitation, to remove them altogether in almost every case. In my opinion, if we are going to lift the restrictions which are placed about this section, we might just as well say to the house, "Let us do away with the principle, so that every woman who marries a soldier who returned from overseas and later died would be entitled to pension." It seems to me, however, that this section, drafted as it is, is one which could be accepted. It restricts in one way, and in another way it is far broader in its operation than any section drafted along the lines of the suggestions made in recent years that there should be a time limitation, or that those who married prior to the coming into force

Pension Act
of the act of 1919 should be entitled to certain benefits. This protects the widow from the time the soldier was wounded, provided the conditions specified herein are adhered to.
After all, we want to be of some practical benefit to the soldier, and I think the committee laboured with that end in view. On four separate occasions amendments to the Pension Act covering this matter were passed by the House of Commons, and were rejected by another house. It is at least possible that if the act seemed too wide, this section would benefit, I would almost say, hundreds of cases, and may appear to our friends in the other house as a less innocuous form. Personally I think it goes very far, and the legislation is at any rate based on a principle other than that of time limitation. Every member of this house knows that that is useless from the standpoint of restriction, and it is also arbitrary. I heartily commend the section to the house, if it is intended to do anything which may be of use to the soldier. With the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark), which makes clear the intent of the act, I think that the section should be accepted as it is, and should be passed. It was fully discussed in the committee. There were different opinions; I think a number of the members did not agree that this is the best possible section, but they all agreed that something should be done for the persons concerned.

As I understand it, the member for Vancouver-Burrard wants to know why it is the burden of proof is placed upon the widow, and that also puzzles me a little. Why should it not be up to the department in the first place? The marriage is proved; it is proved that a member of the forces died; then comes the question, shall the widow be entitled to a pension? Why should she not be entitled? Then you say, "You shall not have a pension unless you can show that prior to marriage you made certain reasonable inquiries, and after that you did not anticipate that the injury or disease would be a specific factor in causing death." When she shows that she was married, and her husband died from the injury, why should it not be up to the department to show that any reasonable inquiry on her part would have disclosed that death would likely result from the injury from which her husband was then suffering? You are putting the burden of proof upon the woman. Why should it not be upon the department, when she once establishes the fact that she was married to a soldier, and that he died from his injury?

Is my hon. friend referring
to the words after the word "provided?"

I am referring to the words
which appear in subsection (iii), paragraph (b) of section 32; section 25 of this bill. I will read it to make it clear:
That a pension shall be paid in the case of a member of the forces who has married and who had died of a pensionable disability prior to the coming into force of this act, if,' at the time of the marriage,-
I understand there is a change there.
the condition of such member of the forces was such that the prospective wife after making reasonable inquiries would not anticipate that the injury or disease would be a substantial factor in causing death.
The point I am trying to make is that the burden of proof should not be put upon the woman in that respect. I do not think any woman would be apt to know anything about this law. I suppose she would satisfy herself that she wanted to marry the man, and perhaps would know that he had some injury or trouble of some kind, but I do not suppose she would go any further, and I do not think she would ever make any such inquiry.
It would be reasonable* for her not to go any further.

I do not think it would be reasonable for her not to do that, when she would not know anything about the law. I will admit that if the man was suffering from an injury or disease which any reasonable person would expect might cause death, perhaps she should not get a pension then if she married him. But my point is that it should be up to the department, and not up to the woman. You say to her: "You have qualified in every way, but you have not made inquiry, and because you have not you must suffer."
I would go so far as to say that it would be reasonable for her to make no inquiry at all and she would be entitled to pension.
I do not think my hon. friend would seriously suggest that any board or commission would come to the conclusion that a person who had made no inquiry had made reasonable inquiry.

I am not opposing this suggestion, as I think iit is of considerable merit, but I made a proposition to the committee that I thought was simpler and probably more effective than this one. ,If you put all the women on an equality and restricted them to the first marriage after discharge, I think you would simplify it. It is something you can justify without any discrimination.
Pension Act

I submit that the hon member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has taken a wrong view of this matter. I understood him to say that he had always been opposed to granting pension to the widow of a soldier who had a pensionable disability at the time of marriage.
Where she married him after the appearance of that disability.

Or who had married the soldier after the appearance of the disability. I think that is going a little too far. I quite agree that in the case of death bed marriages, as they are called, where, for the sake of getting a pension a woman marries a man who is just about to die-if there have been such cases, and I doubt very much if there have been many-she should not be entitled to the pension. In the ordinary case, where a man has a pensionable disability and gets married and has children, a situation arises which, to my mind, constitutes an anomaly. As I understand the act, in such a case there would be a pension allowed in respect of the children, but no pension would be given to the mother of those children. The pension would not be sufficient to enable the mother to pay her full living expenses and also the living expenses of the children; it would be sufficient only to provide for the maintenance of the children. I do not think a marriage of that kind should in any sense be termed a death bed marriage. It was a marriage which took place in the usual way, and there is no question that the mother of the children of a man who fought for this country in the war should receive special consideration.
I have in mind a case which may or may not have been brought to the attention of the committee1-I was not on the committee myself;-where a man and his three sons went to the war voluntarily. One of the sons was killed in the war and there was no pension in respect of him because he was not married. Another son, after I think two years or more of service in the hottest part of the fight, received a pensionable disability and he was invalided back to Canada. On his return he set about pursuing his ordinary occupation and he was able to carry on for some time. He got married; he had three children, and quite recently he died leaving a widow and three children with nothing at all to take care of them except the pension which would be allowed in respect of the children. It is quite true that the man at the time of his marriage

was receiving a pension and I presume it would also be held that in his case his disability constituted a factor in the causes which brought about his death. It seems to me, however, that that is a case which should be provided for and I would suggest that it would be only fair and reasonable for us to provide for payment of a pension to a widow where one or more children are involved. I quite agree with the hon. member for Yan-couver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) that the clause as it reads is not satisfactory, because, as he pointed out, what has to be shown is not that the man was receiving a pension at the time of marriage, but that he had a pensionable disability. That seems to be very unreasonable. I understand that if a pensionable disability existed at the time of the marriage, the widow is not entitled to a pension. I do not think that is what was intended by the committee. It would be more reasonable if it was provided that the man was receiving a pension at the time. In that way the clause would mean something because it is a difficult problem to decide whether the pensionable disability actually existed at the time of the marriage or not. If the man was receiving a pension then of course there could be no dispute about the matter. But even in that case I think the committee has not gone far enough and the people of Canada as a whole are willing that pensions should be allowed on a reasonable scale and that we should not be too technical in considering applications for pensions.
I have had a good deal of experience in dealing with pension cases and I am afraid I shall have to admit that I have come to the conclusion that the pension authorities have adopted a policy to the effect that they will if possible refuse to grant a pension. I do not know whether such instructions were issued or not, but it seems as if they were imbued with the idea that it was their duty to keep down pensions as much as possible. That is not what we should have in this country at all. That is not what the Canadian people desire. I would suggest that we should perhaps go to the other extreme; that we should be liberal in granting pensions and that there should be authority or jurisdiction or power in the pension commission to grant pensions* in cases where there is a real necessity for them.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

Dumping Duty-Mr. Fraser

The house resumed, from Monday, May 14, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for committee of supply, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Anderson (Halton):
That all the words after the word "that" be stricken out and the following substituted therefor:
"In the opinion of this house the necessary action should be taken by the government forthwith to effectively control the importation into Canada, either on sale, or on consignment, of natural products of a class or kind produced in Canada under conditions which prejudicially or injuriously affect, or threaten to prejudicially or injuriously affect, the interests of Canadian producers."

When the house rose last night I had made reference to the declaration of the Prime Minister that what the government objected to in the presentation by the delegation was that they were asking the government to give the Minister of National Revenue and the officials of that department authority and power to fix throughout the year a tariff on the natural products of the Dominion of Canada. I listened very attentively to what the delegation had to say, and let me point out that the delegation made no such request of the government at any time. My observation would lead me to believe that the delegation was a company of reasonable and intelligent people, and that they did not come to Ottawa for the purpose of presenting to the government any request that would make them look foolish. These gentlemen knew perfectly well that they had been enjoying protection by virtue of some statute or regulation or order in council. I quite admit that they may have been confused as to the correct name to give to some of these statutes or regulations or orders in council, but they knew perfectly well that for the two preceding years they had been enjoying certain benefits by virtue of the application of some law or regulation or order. They were also of the opinion that they were entitled to the continuance of the benefits they were receiving under the law or regulation or order, because it is and has been the settled policy of the government of the Dominion of Canada ever since confederation to give protection wherever protection is necessary and reasonable. The manufacturers have been enjoying that privilege for a great number of years, and if the manufacturers are entitled to it, there is no reason why the farmers and producers of all kinds should not be entitled to protection. They may not have had a clear appreciation of the order in council, but they understood perfectly the applies

tion of its cancellation. They knew that their protection had vanished, and they came to Ottawa asking for the restoration of the protection which they had enjoyed.
I make the statement that the Prime Minister in making the statement he did, that this delegation came to Ottawa seeking authority for the customs officials to set a tariff or impose a duty, did not place the request of these gentlemen in the proper light. He put an improper interpretation on the request that had been presented to the government. In addition to that, he practically told them that he did not propose to accede to their request. Let the producers of the Dominion of Canada just analyse the statement which the Prime Minister made on that occasion, and I think they will agree with what I have said. I will quote from the stenographic report of the statement of the Prime Minister. He said:
I hope you will go away feeling that the government is only too delighted to have this opportunity of hearing your representations, and of stating the situation to you in the light of the facts as they are. And what I hope you will carry away with you is the correct impression, not that any statute has been repealed, and not that any power given to the governor in council has been repealed. That all remains, and will continue to remain as it is. All that has been repealed is what we have been obliged to recognize was an interpretation that was leading to extremes, in a manner which, speaking for myself personally, seemed to be highly prejudicial to the very interests that it was intended to safeguard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Hear, hear;
that is all right.

That was the statement
made by the Prime Minister, and I want the producers of this Dominion to note exactly what the Prime Minister states. He states that the statute has not been repealed, that the power given under the order in council has not been repealed, that all remains and will continue to remain as it is. Remember, when the Prime Minister was speaking, the order in council had been repealed, and he makes the statement that it is going to stay repealed, because he says, "and will continue to remain as it is."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. The powers given under the statute remain as they are.
The power of the governor in council has been repealed, and it was repealed at the time the Prime Minister made that statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No; my hon. friend is mistaken. What was repealed was the order in council, not the power given to

the governor in council. The power given to the governor in council remains, but the particular order that the minister recommended under that power was repealed-not the power that the governor in council has.
The order in council has been repealed. Therefore section 6 and section 43 are inoperative.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
That was the effect, and the Prime Minister stated that that state of affairs was going to remain. That is my interpretation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let me give my hon. friend the right interpretation. Section 43 remains in the statute. That section gives certain powers to the governor in council. That section still remains, and those powers still remain. Under that section a certain order was passed by the government, at the instance of the minister. That particular order has been repealed, but the minister to-morrow can bring another recommendation before council and the governor in council can pass an order under the general power that still exists.
I am well aware of that, but, with all deference to the right hon. the Prime Minister, I maintain that when the order in council had been repealed the legislation was inoperative.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, not the legislation.

Yes, the legislation, and
you cannot put it into effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is where the whole confusion has arisen. The legislation is still there which gives the governor in council power to pass any order in council under it.
It is still there, but what good is it? It is not operative. You cannot operate under it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, we can.
No sir, you cannot, without another order in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We could put through another order in council in five minutes.

I do not know that you can. The Prime Minister says that he could put an order in council through in five 
minutes, but he sat in power from 1922 to 1926, and he did not pass such an order in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was no need for it.

No need for it? I know that the fruit growers of British Columbia were complaining during all those years of exactly the same thing, and they were asking for this relief. I still maintain that the statement made by the Prime Minister shows that the legislation is not operative. It is not working, and he says that it is going to remain that way. So the fruit growers of British Columbia cannot look to this government for any remedy under the existing conditions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is quite wrong.
I am sorry, but I must disagree with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is quite
wrong, and the best appeal is to the statute itself. The statute is still there.

That is quite all right. I am not contending that the statute was repealed, but let me ask the Prime Minister this question: Are you going to put into effect another order in council to-morrow, as you state you have power to do?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the very minute the minister comes to council and gives us reasonable grounds for putting that order into effect, the governor in council will I believe act on the advice of the minister.
That will not please the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young).

What are reasonable
grounds?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When the purpose of the statute is to be invoked.

In view of the repeal of the order in council, the legislation is inoperative so far as giving protection to the fruit growers of British Columbia is concerned, and I would ask, what are the chances of the fruit growers getting the benefit of any such order in council and getting the benefit of this legislation provided this government remains in power? We can only judge them by their past performances. This order in council and this statute continued in existence from 1922 to 1926, and the Liberal government of those days made no move to provide the growers of fruit and vegetables with any protection at

Dumping Duty-Mr. Fraser
all. They were voted out of office, and it was not until their successors had got in the saddle that any protection was provided for those engaged in this industry. I challenge any member of the government or any of its officials to deny that statement. I say they sat for four years with this machinery at their disposal, but they absolutely refused to make it effective in any shape or form. Now, do the fruit and vegetable growers of this country expect to get legislation or orders in council from this government to protect their industry?
Was there not a duty of 30 per cent in effect all those years?
I am not talking about the common, ordinary duty at all. I am talking about the application of the special duty under section 6 and section 43, and my hon. friend from Weyburn knows it very well.
The dumping duty goes on without the necessity of an order in council.

Well, the dumping duty
that I am talking about was not on.
You are talking about your own.
No, 1 am talking about the dumping duty under 47a. Now, 43 was not put in operation.
Section 43 cannot and does not provide for a dumping duty.
It provides for a special duty.
No.

You are tangling this thing up so we cannot tell what you are talking about. The fact remains that the Liberal government did not provide any protection for our fruit and vegetable growers, and they will not provide it now. I challenge contradiction of that statement.
There is protection of 90 cents per barrel under the general law.

I am not talking about
that, I am talking about the special, or dumping, duty.
But you are saying-
Order.

Will the hon. gentleman
permit a question?
Certainly.

What is the protection
afforded by the general law on a barrel of apples; how does it compare with the United States tariff?
We do not talk of barrels of apples in British Columbia, we talk of boxes of apples.
My hon. friend knows that the tariff deals with barrels of apples.
Yes.
Does he not know that the tariff is 90 cents per barrel?
I think that is correct.
That is 20 cents higher than the United States tariff-one of the highest tariffs in the world on apples.
What has that got to do with it?
My hon. friend was saying that no protection was afforded, and-
Order.

Now then, the Prime
Minister stated to the delegates that the statute was going to remain as it is. It would have been just a little clearer to them had he added ''as it is and was from 1922 to 1926." Then they would know exactly what he meant, which was that the statute was not going to be put into operation. I interpret the action of the government as an acknowledgment that they are impotent to put into effect that special duty on fruits and vegetables on account of the peculiar situation, half of their support being free trade and the other half protection. The Prime Minister also said that:
The authority under the order in council was applied in a manner which, speaking for myself personally, seemed to be highly prejudicial to the very interests that it was intended to safeguard.
That is, the Prime Minister told the fruit and vegetable growers, after they had been enjoying the benefits of that protection for the last three or four years: You were not enjoying any protection at all; you only thought you were enjoying it. But as a matter of fact they were actually enjoying the protection, because he says here that it was-
[DOT]-highly prejudicial to the very interests that it was intended to safeguard.
Now, I want to ask the fruit and vegetable growers of the Dominion if they think that under the operation of the order in council and the appraisers' bulletins they were pre-
Dumping Duty-M*-. Fraser

judicially affected; or were they benefited. I am confident that every fruit grower will say: Why, for the last two years we admit that we have been enjoying benefits, and that is what we are coming here for. These practical men know perfectly well that they have been enjoying benefits under that condition of affairs. Not only has the producer benefited, but the consumer has not complained of the duties that were imposed under that section. I will refer to this a little later.
I say to the fruit and vegetable growers of the Dominion: As long as this government is in office the powers under those sections of the act are dead and will not be revived. In my opinion the Prime Minister wishes that order in council buried forty feet deep in the fertile soil of fair Saskatchewan, and he certainly will not erect over it a monument with the inscription, Resurgam. He would like to see it buried there forever.

You cannot get me as,
badly balled up as you got the delegation the other day; I have studied it pretty closely since that time.
Now, I should like to address a few remarks to my hon. friend from Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lanctot), who spoke last night on the effect of this section and pleaded eloquently for protection for the fruit and vegetable growers in his section of Quebec. How does he expect to get it from this government? I do not think he has a chance in the world. Under present conditions it is an impossibility for the government to provide it. The translation of his speech appeared this morning, and he said something like this:	After the
session is over I expect to come down to Ottawa with a delegation and put my request before the Government, and I think the Government will see that it is granted. Well, I do not think anything of the kind. I am confident that the government has no intention of restoring the order in council which would bring into operation the special duty. Therefore it seems to me it is impossible for the hon. gentleman to vote against this amendment.
But there is also another angle to this controversy. It is a matter in regard to which the cabinet itself is not of one opinion. That may be all right; I am not finding any fault with it. But I am pointing out to the people of this Dominion the existing conditions so far as the cabinet is concerned in relation to this legislation. You will find in

the same report from which I quoted a few minutes ago a statement made by the Minister of National Revenue towards the close of the delegation's visit. I wish to read that statement, and you will bear in mind that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had stated that the customs officials-the Minister of National Revenue and his officers-were not applying this act as the government had intended, but that they were fixing the tariff throughout the year, and that he did not think this was a proper application of the order in council. What had the Minister of National Revenue to say in that regard?
In the first place, 47a, the law under which the minister could be given authority to fix values, gives the governor in council or the cabinet authority to empower the minister to fix the value.
The Prime Minister in speaking to this delegation emphasized the fact that they were fixing the duty; the Minister of National Revenue says that they are fixing the value.
The authority to fix values is not in council at all. is not in cabinet. The power that is in council is to give the authority to the minister to actually fix the value. I think that should be understood.
The Minister of National Revenue, whose duty it is to interpret the act and to interpret the intention of the government, as well as to apply the act to the existing conditions, gives that interpretation. He says that the law empowered the minister to fix values. He states that the authority to fix values is not in council at all; it is not in the cabinet. The power that is in the council is " to give authority to the minister to actually fix the value" He goes on:
The one misconception, or possible misconception that I would desire to remove is this: that whereas the order in council did give the minister power to fix values, and did not state for what period those values should stand, it should not be assumed that these values were fixed by the minister for the whole year, and they stood all the year round.
That is to say, notwithstanding, as the Prime Minister pointed out, that these officials were to fix the duty for the year round, the Minister of National Revenue declares that such should not be assumed to be the case. He goes on:
The orders in no case, I think, were fixed to stand for a whole year. I think it would be very, very difficult for any minister to come in and say that he has fixed the values to, say, the months of July and August. . . . The whole idea of the minister and his officials is to endeavour to keep those values in force only for such time as such emergency exists. I do not think that there were any instances where it was kept on the year round. I think some of the trouble arose out of this fact: We did

Dumping Duty-Mr. Gershaw
fix the value of lettuce, and through an oversight in the department-and I am quite willing to take responsibility for that-at the time it was recommended to us that the fixed value should be taken off the lettuce, through an oversight it was not done, and that value was left on the lettuce for a period longer than it should have remained. I have no great knowledge of the details of all this, but I do know that the department officials do try to carry out the intention of the law and I think that we have been fairly successful in doing that.... I think we have been fairly successful, from the fact that^ so far as I am aware, there was never any objection made to it on the part of the consumer.
That is what the Minister of National Revenue said. He went on to say:
I do not want the impression to go abroad that values which had been fixed were fixed for the year. We have in this country a Department of National Revenue. We are collectors of revenue; that is practically our job, and this is one of the things that has been wished on it. However, I might say that we have taken the word of those who know the conditions. My friend the Minister of Agriculture advises me that he thinks a duty should be put, or a higher valuation should be put on certain goods, on vegetables, or on eggs, we will say. He makes the recommendation to the Minister of Customs. The Minister of Customs has been merely the instrument in carrying out the desires of that department.
There you have the Minister of National Revenue at variance with the Prime Minister of the country. More than that, the Minister of National Revenue absolutely ties up the Minister of Agriculture as the party responsible for recommending values. He finds that an emergency exists and then he passes on a recommendation as to value, and the Minister of National Revenue imposes it. What about my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell)? 1 thought he came from Saskatchewan. And I thought my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) was from the same province. The hon. member for Weyburn complained that he could not get information. I think there is an explanation. The Minister of Agriculture has been playing the game of hide and seek with Mr. Weyburn, and Mr. Weyburn says, "I spy". That is the explanation. That is why the hon. member could not get his information.
I have just a few more words to say in conclusion. The district I have the honour to represent contains a great number of fruit and vegetable growers. I had the opportunity of passing through the apple district when the order in council was passed in 1926 fixing the price of apples. If the government could get in contact with the people and could realize the satisfaction which they derived from the imposition of that order in council I think they would reconsider this question 56103-194
and again fix the values of these products. The apple growers at that time, from one end of the valley to the other, made the same comment without any variations. They said: "We are glad that that value has been fixed, because we know now that we are going to get a certain minimum for our apples." For the last two years the trouble has been this: We packed and shipped our apples but we did not know whether there would be any return on them. The apple grower shipped these apples, and out of the first receipts he had to pay for these special charges, and in many instances the amount the apples sold for would not cover the charges. The result was that the grower actually had to dig down into his pocket, after cultivating his orchard and gathering and packing his fruit and shipping it. Apart from losing the whole of that fruit he was out of pocket in connection with the cost of these charges. If this government would realize these conditions and look carefully into the situation I believe they would reconsider the passing of the order in council as it applied from 1926 until the other day.

Those who have taken part in this debate have wandered far afield and the discussion has developed into a free for all on the old subject of the tariff. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) last night, in his clear and concise way, quoted at length from a letter written by the Secretary of the Medicine Hat chamber of commerce. I wish to say that this chamber is not a partisan body, and I am sure it has no desire or intention to provide campaign propaganda for any political party. I am sure also that it would be the very last body to claim that it represented the real feeling of the majority of the people in that district. There are many people there -consumers'-who believe that they should have the privilege and the opportunity of purchasing fruits and vegetables, when they come in, at reasonable prices and not at prices greatly enhanced by the tariff.
It seems that a wrong impression has gone abroad in two respects, and I believe that impression has been due to the material which has been broadcast so generally on one aspect of this question. The first impression, which in my opinion is wrong, is that the members of the Liberal and Progressive groups are not looking after the interests of the producers, the farmers. These groups, I might mention, were some years ago responsible for retaining the Crowsnest rates. These rates constitute the bill of rights of the Canadian shipper and have resulted in the

Dumping Duty-Mr. Gershaw

saving of much money annually to those producers in the prairie provinces. Since the imposition of the Fordney-McCumber tariff against our cattle, grain and other farm products, farmers generally are realizing that we need wider markets, and consequently we have been constantly searching for such markets for our products. Not so long ago the Liberal party went down to defeat in an endeavour to secure a reciprocity arrangement with the United States to give wider markets to our producers.
The second impression which has gone abroad, and which is not correct, is that early fruits and vegetables come in free of duty. Now, let me say that, rain or shine, in season or out of season, this parliament maintains a duty against the importation of these commodities. It is mentioned by the Minister of Finance last night, and I repeat the list now. The duty on apples is ninety cents a barrel; the duty on blackberries, gooseberries, raspberries and strawberries two cents per pound; and all other green fruit not provided for 25 per cent; cabbages, 30 per cent; potatoes, 35 per cent; tomatoes, 30 per cent; turnips, 30 per cent; and vegetables not otherwise provided for 30 per cent. These rates seem to me to be fairly substantial. In addition, it is quite clear that the government, who possibly at most removed the power which the minister or some officer in the department had, at a stroke of the pen, of changing the value or increasing it for duty purposes, surely have the power to impose that duty again by order in council at any time. I believe that the tariff in this respect may work in a way which is of no benefit to the producer, and it will certainly increase prices to the consumer. One case was mentioned last night where the peach producers sold 50,000 boxes of peaches in the prairie provinces, and yet the people had to pay a duty on something like 400,000 boxes, which was the amount used. It seems to me that in the interests of the people generally, this dumping clause should be invoked only when very special conditions arise; and I believe that in connection with such things as food products, and especially fresh fruits and vegetables, which are so necessary to the health of the people, the dumping duty should be imposed-in addition to the duties which are always in existence-only when very exceptional conditions arise.

If we pay a little more for our apples; if we pay a little more for our eggs, or a little more for our butter, it will be worth it. I know the working men of British Columbia are willing to do so. We want the purchasing power, and we do not mind paying good prices. If the farmers succeed; if the vegetable growers succeed, and if the poultry men succeed, they will erect buildings and give work to carpenters, painters and plasterers. They, in turn, will erect buildings, and that is how an industrial community is built up.
There is no argument at all against a seasonal tariff on vegetables coming into this country. There is no argument against an effective duty on eggs coming into this country from the United States. Take the case of butter and eggs alone. When we entered into that very foolish

I won't say treaty-arrangement with New Zealand, which gave the same terms to them as were embodied in the treaty with Australia, we in British Columbia were going through a rather trying time. The dairymen had not succeeded, but times were getting better. Wages were improving, and people were eating more butter, and the dairymen began to succeed. When we entered into this treaty with Australia the Americans saw the danger. They had a duty of 8 cents a pound against us for butter, but, notwithstanding that duty, in 1925 we sent over $2,500,000 worth of butter to the United States. They saw that butter would be coming in from New Zealand, and they immediately placed a duty of 12 cents a pound on that commodity. That meant that we lost that $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 of trade with the United States, and the arrangement with New Zealand meant that 14,000,000 pounds of butter came into British Columbia and Halifax in seven months. That meant disaster to the dairy people. As has been stated in this house more eloquently than I can put it, all through Ontario they sold their stock, and in British Columbia they went out of the dairy business. If you go there now you will see them going out of the poultry business just the same.
Why, Mr. Speaker, can we not take a leaf out of the book of the people south of us? We have been acting as an immigration agent for them for years. They have attracted our people; they have been getting our population. We spend millions of dollars to induce people to come and settle in Canada. We can bring about the repatriation of many of our people; the members from Quebec can

bring back thirty or forty thousand of their compatriots if they would just agree to adopt legislation along the lines I am so clumsily trying to place before you to-night. We have the raw material here; we have a great agricultural country, and we have many other resources.
